documents.title: Dataset Construction and DQ Assessment – Residential Real Estate Mortgages

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction of the reference data set (RDS) for the PD-MORT-NL v4 model and the assessment of its data quality. It follows the RDS template of MRM-STD-021 and was approved by the Head of Retail Credit Risk Modelling on 12 June 2027 (document version 1.0).

sections.heading: Range of application and intended use
sections.text: The RDS serves exclusively the PD-MORT-NL v4 rating system, which assigns 12-month PDs to Dutch residential mortgage loans to private individuals. The range of application covers owner-occupied residential mortgages originated in the Netherlands under the Bank's own label and through intermediaries, including the facilities of the former brand portfolio that were migrated in 2011; buy-to-let mortgages and mortgages to legal entities are outside the range of application and are covered by other rating systems. All facilities in the range of application are exposures to natural persons secured by residential immovable property, managed on a pooled basis, and are assigned to the retail exposure class by the Bank's exposure class assignment engine in accordance with CRR Art. 147(5) and the documented assignment sequence of the exposure class methodology. The primary use of the resulting PDs is the calculation of own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach; the secondary use is the prioritisation of arrears management and early-warning monitoring in Retail Collections, which concerns the same population and uses the same RDS.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The reference data set covers monthly snapshots from January 2012 to December 2024, totalling 9.6 million account-months for 780,000 unique facilities.

evidence.quote: monthly snapshots from January 2012 to December 2024

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window was chosen to maximise the available history after the migration to the current mortgage administration system in 2011. It includes the 2012–2013 housing market downturn and the low-default period 2016–2021.

evidence.quote: includes the 2012–2013 housing market downturn

sections.heading: Composition of the observation sample
sections.text: The monthly source snapshots are retained in full in the staging layer of the risk data warehouse. To limit serial dependence between observations of the same facility, the build code retains for each facility one monthly snapshot per calendar half-year, drawn at random with the fixed seed 20260915. The resulting RDS contains 9,600,412 account-months for 780,000 unique facilities of 341,600 unique obligors, of which 43,118 account-months are followed by a default of the obligor within the 12-month outcome window (account-month default rate 0.45%). The outcome window of the December 2024 snapshots ends on 31 December 2025, the last month for which default data were final when the source snapshots were extracted on 15 January 2027. Over the observation period 9,480 obligor-level default events occurred, covering 21,370 facilities. The number of defaults per calibration segment is sufficient for estimation and calibration: segment S1 (no arrears in the previous 12 months) contains 9,468,606 account-months with 28,348 subsequent defaults and segment S2 (arrears in the previous 12 months) 131,806 account-months with 14,770 subsequent defaults.

sections.heading: Length of the observation period
sections.text: The observation period of 13 years exceeds the minimum of five years required by CRR Art. 180(2)(e) for retail PD estimation and forms one continuous time span that includes the five most recent years and all earlier years for which facility-level default data are available in the current mortgage administration system. Data from the predecessor system (1998–2011) were not migrated at facility level; only aggregate annual arrears statistics exist for that period and they are not used for estimation. One-year default rates per calendar year, computed as the average of the four quarter-end reference dates of that year on the full monthly snapshots, are: 2012 0.84%, 2013 0.93%, 2014 0.79%, 2015 0.61%, 2016 0.43%, 2017 0.34%, 2018 0.28%, 2019 0.25%, 2020 0.23%, 2021 0.19%, 2022 0.21%, 2023 0.26% and 2024 0.34%. The highest one-year default rate of the available history (0.93%, 2013) lies within the observation period, so no year with a higher observed default rate has been excluded.

sections.heading: Calculation of one-year default rates
sections.text: One-year default rates are calculated at each quarter-end from March 2012 to December 2024 with overlapping one-year windows: the denominator comprises all obligors in the range of application that are not in default at the reference date and hold at least one credit obligation, and the numerator those that default at least once during the following 12 months. An obligor that defaults more than once within a window is counted only once in the numerator and once in the denominator. Obligors that fully repay, refinance with another lender, are written off or migrate to another rating system during the window remain in the calculation; the resulting bias was analysed and is negligible (−0.004 percentage points on the long-run average), because early redemptions are concentrated among low-risk obligors. Observations are removed from the numerator only where the default was wrongly flagged (technical past due cases corrected in the default register, 214 obligor-windows) and from numerator and denominator only where the facility was wrongly assigned to the range of application (buy-to-let loans recorded as owner-occupied, 1,106 obligor-windows). Obligors in the range of application without a PD-MORT-NL grade at the reference date, mainly loans in their first month after origination, are included in the default rate calculation as a separate unrated category (0.3% of obligors). Default rates per grade use the grade after overrides, exclude conservative adjustments and ignore the substitution effect of NHG guarantees. Obligors are identified by the group-wide customer identifier across the mortgage administration system and the arrears management system, so that each obligor is counted only once even where its facilities are recorded in both systems.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: The components of the definition of default of CR-STD-110 (days-past-due counters with materiality thresholds, UTP flags and probation status) have been captured in the Bank's source systems since 1 January 2016. For snapshots from January 2021 the default flag is taken directly from the default register maintained under CR-STD-110 v2.0. For January 2016 to December 2020, when CR-STD-110 v1.0 applied, the build code re-derives the past-due default from the captured daily days-past-due components, applying the current materiality threshold of EUR 100 and 1% instead of the threshold of CR-STD-110 v1.0, so that historical data are adjusted to the definition of default of EBA/GL/2016/07. For January 2012 to December 2015 the default flag is approximated at obligor level: an obligor is flagged when the arrears management system shows more than three monthly instalments in arrears with an arrears amount above EUR 100, or when a distressed restructuring, forced sale or bankruptcy code is recorded. The three regimes (approximated 2012–2015, re-derived 2016–2020, register 2021–2025) are analysed separately, and the RDS field DOD_REGIME (values APPROX, V1_ADJ and V2) identifies the regime under which each default flag was derived. The regulatory materiality threshold under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and ECB Regulation (EU) 2018/1845 has applied in the default register since 31 December 2020, and the RDS field MAT_REG_FLAG identifies the observations from that date onwards. The effect of the approximation on default rates and its treatment in the estimates are addressed in the model development document.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: A facility is flagged as defaulted when it is more than 90 days past due above a materiality threshold of EUR 100 absolute and 1% relative, or when an unlikeliness-to-pay trigger is met.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: UTP triggers comprise distressed restructuring, forced sale of the collateral, bankruptcy of the obligor and specific credit risk adjustments. Triggers are sourced from the arrears management system and applied at obligor level.

evidence.quote: UTP triggers comprise distressed restructuring, forced sale of the collateral, bankruptcy

sections.heading: Level of application and joint obligations
sections.text: The definition of default is applied at obligor level, in line with CR-STD-110 §4.2 and with the Bank's retail risk management practice, in which arrears management, forbearance and collections are organised per household; all facilities of a defaulted obligor are flagged as defaulted in the RDS. The level of application has not changed over the observation period: the approximated flag for 2012–2015 is also constructed at obligor level by aggregating arrears over all facilities of the obligor. Joint mortgage loans of two partners are treated as a separate obligor (the joint obligor) in the materiality threshold calculation, and the default of a joint obligation is propagated to the individual credit obligations of both partners in accordance with CR-STD-110 §4.3 and section 8 of EBA/GL/2016/07. Of the 9,480 obligor-level default events, 6,215 concern joint obligors, and 38 default events of individual partners result from the propagation of a joint default. Because the definition is applied at obligor level, the facility-level provisions of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and of EBA/GL/2016/07 are not used.

sections.heading: Days-past-due counting and materiality threshold
sections.text: Since 2016 the days-past-due counter is calculated daily in the arrears management system; it starts on the first day on which both the absolute component (EUR 100) and the relative component (1%) of the materiality threshold are exceeded and restarts when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, including current accounts and consumer loans, and the relative component is that sum divided by the total on-balance-sheet exposure to the obligor, excluding equity exposures. The thresholds applied are those set by the ECB for retail exposures of all significant institutions (EUR 100 and 1%); no lower internal threshold is used. An obligor is flagged as defaulted under the past-due criterion at the onset of the 91st consecutive day on which both components are exceeded, and the default date recorded in the RDS is the first day on which any default criterion is met. Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date is recognised as past due, and where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the basis of the modified schedule. All amounts are denominated in euro, so the currency provision of Art. 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 does not apply.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness to pay in the RDS
sections.text: The RDS takes the UTP flags from the default register of the arrears management system, which applies the automatic triggers of CR-STD-110 §6.1: non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments including Stage 3 classification, sale at a credit-related economic loss above 5%, distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy (including WSNP debt restructuring) and forced sale of the collateral. Case-by-case UTP assessments (for example fraud, a significant decline in household income or repeated forbearance) are recorded in the default register with outcome, rationale and date, and 1,142 of the 9,480 default events originate from such an assessment. The operationalisation of every trigger, including source-system fields and responsibilities, is documented in the Definition of Default implementation memo (version 1.0, 15 March 2027) and summarised in Annex A. Default events by first trigger: 90 days past due 71.8%, distressed restructuring 14.6%, case-by-case UTP 12.0%, forced sale and bankruptcy 1.6%.

sections.heading: Consistency with other uses of the default definition
sections.text: The default flag in the RDS for 2021–2025 is identical to the default status used for IFRS 9 Stage 3, for non-performing exposure reporting and in the LGD-MORT-NL model, so that the same definition of default is applied to the same historical observations in the PD and LGD models of the rating system. Where the accounting concept of credit-impaired and the prudential default status could diverge, the RDS carries them in distinct fields (IFRS9_STAGE and DEFAULT_FLAG_CRR), and the quarterly reconciliations described in §6.6 show no divergence since January 2021. All Dutch residential mortgages of the Bank are administered by one legal entity, so a single definition of default applies to all exposures in the range of application and no subsidiary uses a different definition. Consistency of the internal definition with CRR Art. 178, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and EBA/GL/2016/07 is demonstrated in the mapping table of section 13 of the Definition of Default implementation memo.

sections.heading: Data dictionary and critical data elements
sections.text: Annex A contains the data dictionary with, for each of the 38 candidate variables and each of the 11 fields used to construct the default flag, the business definition, the technical definition, the source system, table and field, the transformation and the lineage. All 38 candidate variables and all data elements used to construct the target (default flag, default date, default trigger, days-past-due counter, arrears amount and probation status) are designated as critical data elements. Each critical data element has a documented business and technical definition and at least one DQ rule for each applicable dimension of MRM-STD-022 §3, listed in Annex A and implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool. The metadata of every element (business and technical definition, type and format, permitted values, unit and currency, source, Data Owner, update frequency and classification) are recorded in the Group Data Catalogue, and catalogue entries are versioned so that the definition valid at any historical snapshot can be retrieved.

sections.heading: Lineage, transformations and manual inputs
sections.text: For every variable the lineage in Annex A identifies the source system and fields, the intermediate stores (the risk data warehouse and the modelling staging area), each transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the build script and function in repository rds-mort-nl, and the monthly extraction frequency and timing. sections.heading: Data ownership and change control
sections.text: Each of the three data domains from which the RDS is sourced (Mortgage Contracts, Arrears and Collections, Collateral) has exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: the Director Mortgage Operations, the Head of Retail Collections and the Head of Collateral Management respectively. The model owner agreed the data quality expectations for the critical data elements with the three Data Owners in data sharing agreements DSA-2026-044 to DSA-2026-046, signed between 12 and 19 October 2026. Changes to the definition, source or transformation logic of a data element used by the model require approval of the Data Owner and advance notification to the model owner through the data change process; no such change occurred between the extraction of the source snapshots and the approval of this document. The Data Stewards of the three domains own the DQ rules in the Group DQ monitoring tool, and the data management team of the risk data warehouse (IT) is responsible for the technical operation of the extraction jobs.

sections.heading: Use of internal and external data
sections.text: Internal data of the Bank are the only source of default characteristics; no external, pooled or vendor default data are used for risk differentiation or calibration. External inputs are limited to the house-price index used to index collateral values and to automated valuations; their fitness for use is assessed in §6.5, and neither affects the definition of default. The data are extracted from the three source systems through the risk data warehouse, which also feeds the COREP and FINREP reporting, and the aggregation of the model data is fully automated. The risk data warehouse runs the monthly extraction jobs within five business days after month-end; no deviation from the production schedule was observed for the snapshots used in this RDS.

sections.heading: Storage, retention and archiving
sections.text: The frozen RDS (identifier RDS-MORT-NL-v4.0, frozen on 26 February 2027) is stored read-only in the protected zone of the analytics platform together with the build code tag, the lineage and the metadata extract, so that the development data can be reproduced. Archived RDS versions are protected against alteration by write-once storage, and any correction is made on a new RDS version while the original is retained. RDS versions are retained for the life of the model and for ten years after its decommissioning in accordance with DATA-POL-001 §10.2, with personal data anonymised as described in §7.2. Rating histories, grade assignments, estimated PDs per grade, default events and defaulted exposures with their grade in the year before default are retained in the risk data warehouse from January 2012 onwards, exceeding the observation periods required by CRR Articles 176 and 180. Because each observation carries the risk-driver values of its own monthly snapshot, the RDS contains the risk drivers at the relevant points in time, including for defaulted obligors the snapshots in the 12 months before default.

sections.heading: Changes in lending standards, collection practice and legal environment
sections.text: Lending standards changed materially during the observation period: the statutory LTV limit was reduced from 106% in 2012 by one percentage point per year to 100% in 2018, and since 1 January 2013 new loans must amortise at least on an annuity basis to qualify for mortgage interest deductibility. The RDS was split at 1 January 2013 into facilities originated before and after the change: loans originated from 2013 have a lower average LTV at origination (84% against 92%) and a lower interest-only share (11% against 49% of the balance), and their 12-month arrears incidence is lower in every loan-age band. Collections were centralised in 2016 with an earlier first contact (day 5 instead of day 15 of arrears); cure rates from 30 days past due rose from 58% to 67%, which is captured by the arrears-history risk drivers rather than by a break in the default rate series. No change in Dutch insolvency or foreclosure law with an effect on the default definition occurred in the observation period; debt restructuring under the WSNP procedure is captured as a bankruptcy trigger throughout.

sections.heading: Economic conditions in the observation period
sections.text: The observation period covers the end of the Dutch housing market correction (house prices fell by 6.3% in 2012 and 6.6% in 2013 before recovering from mid-2013), the peak in unemployment of 7.4% in 2014, the expansion of 2015–2019, the COVID-19 period with temporary payment deferrals for 1,870 facilities in 2020, and the interest-rate increases of 2022–2023 with the temporary house-price decline of 2023. Current and foreseeable conditions (high house prices, low unemployment and mortgage rates above the 2015–2021 level) are within the range observed in the RDS; the interest-rate level of 2023–2024 was last observed in 2012. The effect of the payment deferrals of 2020 on the default rate series is assessed in the model development document.

sections.heading: DQ rules and thresholds
sections.text: The DQ rules for the 49 critical data elements (38 candidate variables and 11 default-flag components) were defined jointly by the model developers and the Data Stewards; 212 rules are documented in Annex A and 164 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool. Each rule has an amber and a red threshold equal to or stricter than the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3: completeness below 98% and 95% non-missing, reconciliation differences above 0.5% and 1% of the amount, and consistency below 99% and 98% of records passing. For the target variable and its constituents the thresholds are stricter: 100% completeness of the default flag and default date, and a red threshold of 0.1% for unmatched default events in the reconciliation to the default register. No threshold less strict than the default was applied, so no deviation required approval under MRM-STD-022 §4.5. Data quality of the RDS is managed in accordance with MRM-STD-022, and all DQ results are produced by versioned code from the frozen RDS.

sections.heading: DQ results per dimension
sections.text: Record-level completeness was confirmed by comparing the number of facilities, obligors and default events per snapshot with the mortgage administration system and the default register, and attribute-level completeness is at least 99.4% for all critical data elements except debt-to-income at origination (97.7%, amber, see §4.3). Accuracy was measured by reconciling outstanding balances to the general ledger at each year-end (maximum difference 0.08%) and default events to the default register (§6.6), and by the sample-based verification in §6.5. Consistency was checked between the three source systems, between related fields (for example origination date before snapshot date, arrears amount not exceeding the outstanding balance) and over the observation period, including the change of the default definition in 2016; 99.7% of records pass all logical consistency rules. Validity (permitted values and ranges) and uniqueness (one record per facility and snapshot) are met for 100% of records after the build, and appropriateness for the range of application is assessed in chapter 5. The DQ assessment report in Annex D lists the result of each rule per variable and dimension against its thresholds, and the number and share of records excluded per exclusion reason. The gaps identified, namely the amber completeness of debt-to-income at origination and the approximated default flag before 2016, are explained in §4.3 and §6.2, and their effect on the reliability of the estimates is assessed in the data deficiency log (§6.7).

sections.heading: Sample-based verification and collateral data
sections.text: As required for Tier 1 models, a random sample of 400 facilities was verified against the credit files and valuation reports in the document management system; the accuracy of LTV at origination, income at origination and valuation date was 99.0%, 98.5% and 99.5% respectively, and the 12 deviations found were corrected at source by Mortgage Operations. Collateral data (type, value, valuation date and method, lien rank and link to the secured facilities) are held in the collateral valuation database and meet the completeness and consistency thresholds of MRM-STD-022 for all snapshots after the migration of June 2019; for earlier snapshots the valuation method is missing for 3.1% of collateral records, which does not affect the indexed LTV. Residential properties are valued independently at origination, indexed quarterly with the regional price index and revalued at least every three years or upon a credit event, in accordance with CR-POL-001 §8.3. The house-price index and the automated valuations were compared with 2,450 full valuations obtained in 2023–2024; the median absolute deviation of the indexed value is 6.8%, with no systematic bias by province.

sections.heading: Reconciliation of the default flag and key amounts
sections.text: For default events from January 2021 the RDS default flag was reconciled to the default register maintained under CR-STD-110: 2,146 of 2,151 obligor-level default events match on obligor and default date, and the five differences are technical past due cases corrected in the register after the source extraction and removed from the RDS. IRB and IFRS 9 default flags are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems by Credit Risk Reporting, and the reconciliations for 2021–2024 show no difference in the obligors flagged as defaulted. Outstanding balances and record counts per reference date were reconciled to the general ledger and to the COREP exposure data at each year-end; differences are below 0.1% of the balance and are explained by accrued interest booked on separate accounts. Default status is recorded at obligor level in the arrears management system and propagated daily to the mortgage administration system and the risk data warehouse, so that all facilities of a defaulted obligor carry the default flag in all systems from the same date.

sections.heading: Personal data attributes, lawful basis and purpose limitation
sections.text: The RDS contains 19 personal data attributes of natural persons, listed in Annex A with their purpose in the model, the lawful basis, the pseudonymisation applied and the retention period. An attribute is retained only where it is a candidate risk driver or is needed to construct the default flag or the observation structure; of 31 attributes initially requested, 12 were removed in the data minimisation review of 4 November 2026 (among others marital status, number of children and employer name). Processing for model development, validation and application is based on Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR, as it is necessary for compliance with the Bank's legal obligations under CRR Articles 144, 179 and 180, and this lawful basis was recorded before processing started. The data were originally collected for the conclusion and administration of mortgage contracts, and the compatibility of their reuse for IRB modelling was assessed under Art. 6(4) GDPR in the DPIA, considering the link between the purposes, the context of collection, the nature of the data, the possible consequences for data subjects and the pseudonymisation applied. The processing is recorded in the Record of Processing as RoP-RISK-0231 with its purposes, data categories, recipients, absence of transfers and retention periods, and the model inventory record of MDL-01 references this entry.

sections.heading: Pseudonymisation, security, transfers and retention
sections.text: The RDS is pseudonymised: customer and facility numbers are replaced by keyed tokens generated by the Data Protection Services team, which holds the keys separately from the modelling environment. Re-identification requires a request to Data Protection Services for a documented purpose approved by the Privacy Office and is logged; one request (the file verification of §6.5) was approved on 2 February 2027. The RDS is held in the approved secure analytics environment of the Risk function with role-based access restricted to 14 named staff of Retail Credit Risk Modelling and Model Validation – Credit Risk, logging of all access and encryption at rest. Test environments of the production implementation use masked data derived from the RDS; no production personal data are copied to test environments. All processing takes place in the Bank's data centres in the Netherlands, and no personal data are transferred outside the EEA or to third-party AI services. Personal data in the RDS and development snapshots are retained for the period of use of PD-MORT-NL v4 plus five years after its decommissioning; thereafter they are deleted or irreversibly anonymised and the deletion is evidenced in the retention log of the analytics platform, and the monthly staging snapshots not retained in the RDS are deleted six months after the RDS freeze.

sections.heading: Protected attributes and proxy screening
sections.text: Nationality, gender, ethnicity, religion and health data are not included in the RDS, and no special categories of personal data under Art. 9(1) GDPR are processed. Borrower age is retained only for proxy screening and outcome testing and was not offered as a candidate risk driver, because its use was not approved by Credit Risk Management under CR-POL-001 §9.2. Proxy screening measured the association of each candidate variable with gender (taken from a separate access-restricted extract that is not part of the RDS) and with age band using Cramér's V; only postcode exceeded the screening threshold of 0.15 (V = 0.19 with age band), and it is therefore used solely at provincial level within the house-price index, which is the minimum aggregation needed for collateral indexation. The results of the proxy screening are documented in Annex B.5 of this document, and the outcome testing of the final model is documented in section 7.5 of the model development document.

sections.heading: Range of application and intended use
sections.text: The RDS serves exclusively the PD-MORT-NL v4 rating system, which assigns 12-month PDs to Dutch residential mortgage loans to private individuals. The range of application covers owner-occupied residential mortgages originated in the Netherlands under the Bank's own label and through intermediaries, including the facilities of the former brand portfolio that were migrated in 2011; buy-to-let mortgages and mortgages to legal entities are outside the range of application and are covered by other rating systems. All facilities in the range of application are exposures to natural persons secured by residential immovable property, managed on a pooled basis, and are assigned to the retail exposure class by the Bank's exposure class assignment engine in accordance with CRR Art. 147(5) and the documented assignment sequence of the exposure class methodology. The primary use of the resulting PDs is the calculation of own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach; the secondary use is the prioritisation of arrears management and early-warning monitoring in Retail Collections, which concerns the same population and uses the same RDS.

sections.heading: Composition of the observation sample
sections.text: The monthly source snapshots are retained in full in the staging layer of the risk data warehouse. To limit serial dependence between observations of the same facility, the build code retains for each facility one monthly snapshot per calendar half-year, drawn at random with the fixed seed 20260915. The resulting RDS contains 9,600,412 account-months for 780,000 unique facilities of 341,600 unique obligors, of which 43,118 account-months are followed by a default of the obligor within the 12-month outcome window (account-month default rate 0.45%). The outcome window of the December 2024 snapshots ends on 31 December 2025, the last month for which default data were final when the source snapshots were extracted on 15 January 2027. Over the observation period 9,480 obligor-level default events occurred, covering 21,370 facilities. The number of defaults per calibration segment is sufficient for estimation and calibration: segment S1 (no arrears in the previous 12 months) contains 9,468,606 account-months with 28,348 subsequent defaults and segment S2 (arrears in the previous 12 months) 131,806 account-months with 14,770 subsequent defaults.

sections.heading: Length of the observation period
sections.text: The observation period of 13 years exceeds the minimum of five years required by CRR Art. 180(2)(e) for retail PD estimation and forms one continuous time span that includes the five most recent years and all earlier years for which facility-level default data are available in the current mortgage administration system. Data from the predecessor system (1998–2011) were not migrated at facility level; only aggregate annual arrears statistics exist for that period and they are not used for estimation. One-year default rates per calendar year, computed as the average of the four quarter-end reference dates of that year on the full monthly snapshots, are: 2012 0.84%, 2013 0.93%, 2014 0.79%, 2015 0.61%, 2016 0.43%, 2017 0.34%, 2018 0.28%, 2019 0.25%, 2020 0.23%, 2021 0.19%, 2022 0.21%, 2023 0.26% and 2024 0.34%. The highest one-year default rate of the available history (0.93%, 2013) lies within the observation period, so no year with a higher observed default rate has been excluded.

sections.heading: Calculation of one-year default rates
sections.text: One-year default rates are calculated at each quarter-end from March 2012 to December 2024 with overlapping one-year windows: the denominator comprises all obligors in the range of application that are not in default at the reference date and hold at least one credit obligation, and the numerator those that default at least once during the following 12 months. An obligor that defaults more than once within a window is counted only once in the numerator and once in the denominator. Obligors that fully repay, refinance with another lender, are written off or migrate to another rating system during the window remain in the calculation; the resulting bias was analysed and is negligible (−0.004 percentage points on the long-run average), because early redemptions are concentrated among low-risk obligors. Observations are removed from the numerator only where the default was wrongly flagged (technical past due cases corrected in the default register, 214 obligor-windows) and from numerator and denominator only where the facility was wrongly assigned to the range of application (buy-to-let loans recorded as owner-occupied, 1,106 obligor-windows). Obligors in the range of application without a PD-MORT-NL grade at the reference date, mainly loans in their first month after origination, are included in the default rate calculation as a separate unrated category (0.3% of obligors). Default rates per grade use the grade after overrides, exclude conservative adjustments and ignore the substitution effect of NHG guarantees. Obligors are identified by the group-wide customer identifier across the mortgage administration system and the arrears management system, so that each obligor is counted only once even where its facilities are recorded in both systems.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: The components of the definition of default of CR-STD-110 (days-past-due counters with materiality thresholds, UTP flags and probation status) have been captured in the Bank's source systems since 1 January 2016. For snapshots from January 2021 the default flag is taken directly from the default register maintained under CR-STD-110 v2.0. For January 2016 to December 2020, when CR-STD-110 v1.0 applied, the build code re-derives the past-due default from the captured daily days-past-due components, applying the current materiality threshold of EUR 100 and 1% instead of the threshold of CR-STD-110 v1.0, so that historical data are adjusted to the definition of default of EBA/GL/2016/07. For January 2012 to December 2015 the default flag is approximated at obligor level: an obligor is flagged when the arrears management system shows more than three monthly instalments in arrears with an arrears amount above EUR 100, or when a distressed restructuring, forced sale or bankruptcy code is recorded. The three regimes (approximated 2012–2015, re-derived 2016–2020, register 2021–2025) are analysed separately, and the RDS field DOD_REGIME (values APPROX, V1_ADJ and V2) identifies the regime under which each default flag was derived. The regulatory materiality threshold under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and ECB Regulation (EU) 2018/1845 has applied in the default register since 31 December 2020, and the RDS field MAT_REG_FLAG identifies the observations from that date onwards. The effect of the approximation on default rates and its treatment in the estimates are addressed in the model development document.

sections.text: UTP triggers comprise distressed restructuring, forced sale of the collateral, bankruptcy of the obligor and specific credit risk adjustments. Triggers are sourced from the arrears management system and applied at obligor level.

sections.heading: Level of application and joint obligations
sections.text: The definition of default is applied at obligor level, in line with CR-STD-110 §4.2 and with the Bank's retail risk management practice, in which arrears management, forbearance and collections are organised per household; all facilities of a defaulted obligor are flagged as defaulted in the RDS. The level of application has not changed over the observation period: the approximated flag for 2012–2015 is also constructed at obligor level by aggregating arrears over all facilities of the obligor. Joint mortgage loans of two partners are treated as a separate obligor (the joint obligor) in the materiality threshold calculation, and the default of a joint obligation is propagated to the individual credit obligations of both partners in accordance with CR-STD-110 §4.3 and section 8 of EBA/GL/2016/07. Of the 9,480 obligor-level default events, 6,215 concern joint obligors, and 38 default events of individual partners result from the propagation of a joint default. Because the definition is applied at obligor level, the facility-level provisions of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and of EBA/GL/2016/07 are not used.

sections.heading: Days-past-due counting and materiality threshold
sections.text: Since 2016 the days-past-due counter is calculated daily in the arrears management system; it starts on the first day on which both the absolute component (EUR 100) and the relative component (1%) of the materiality threshold are exceeded and restarts when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, including current accounts and consumer loans, and the relative component is that sum divided by the total on-balance-sheet exposure to the obligor, excluding equity exposures. The thresholds applied are those set by the ECB for retail exposures of all significant institutions (EUR 100 and 1%); no lower internal threshold is used. An obligor is flagged as defaulted under the past-due criterion at the onset of the 91st consecutive day on which both components are exceeded, and the default date recorded in the RDS is the first day on which any default criterion is met. Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date is recognised as past due, and where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the basis of the modified schedule. All amounts are denominated in euro, so the currency provision of Art. 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 does not apply.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness to pay in the RDS
sections.text: The RDS takes the UTP flags from the default register of the arrears management system, which applies the automatic triggers of CR-STD-110 §6.1: non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments including Stage 3 classification, sale at a credit-related economic loss above 5%, distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy (including WSNP debt restructuring) and forced sale of the collateral. Case-by-case UTP assessments (for example fraud, a significant decline in household income or repeated forbearance) are recorded in the default register with outcome, rationale and date, and 1,142 of the 9,480 default events originate from such an assessment. The operationalisation of every trigger, including source-system fields and responsibilities, is documented in the Definition of Default implementation memo (version 1.0, 15 March 2027) and summarised in Annex A. Default events by first trigger: 90 days past due 71.8%, distressed restructuring 14.6%, case-by-case UTP 12.0%, forced sale and bankruptcy 1.6%.

sections.heading: Consistency with other uses of the default definition
sections.text: The default flag in the RDS for 2021–2025 is identical to the default status used for IFRS 9 Stage 3, for non-performing exposure reporting and in the LGD-MORT-NL model, so that the same definition of default is applied to the same historical observations in the PD and LGD models of the rating system. Where the accounting concept of credit-impaired and the prudential default status could diverge, the RDS carries them in distinct fields (IFRS9_STAGE and DEFAULT_FLAG_CRR), and the quarterly reconciliations described in §6.6 show no divergence since January 2021. All Dutch residential mortgages of the Bank are administered by one legal entity, so a single definition of default applies to all exposures in the range of application and no subsidiary uses a different definition. Consistency of the internal definition with CRR Art. 178, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and EBA/GL/2016/07 is demonstrated in the mapping table of section 13 of the Definition of Default implementation memo.

sections.heading: Use of internal and external data
sections.text: Internal data of the Bank are the only source of default characteristics; no external, pooled or vendor default data are used for risk differentiation or calibration. External inputs are limited to the house-price index used to index collateral values and to automated valuations; their fitness for use is assessed in §6.5, and neither affects the definition of default. The data are extracted from the three source systems through the risk data warehouse, which also feeds the COREP and FINREP reporting, and the aggregation of the model data is fully automated. The risk data warehouse runs the monthly extraction jobs within five business days after month-end; no deviation from the production schedule was observed for the snapshots used in this RDS.

Archived RDS versions are protected against alteration by write-once storage, and any correction is made on a new RDS version while the original is retained. RDS versions are retained for the life of the model and for ten years after its decommissioning in accordance with DATA-POL-001 §10.2, with personal data anonymised as described in §7.2. sections.heading: Changes in lending standards, collection practice and legal environment
sections.text: Lending standards changed materially during the observation period: the statutory LTV limit was reduced from 106% in 2012 by one percentage point per year to 100% in 2018, and since 1 January 2013 new loans must amortise at least on an annuity basis to qualify for mortgage interest deductibility. The RDS was split at 1 January 2013 into facilities originated before and after the change: loans originated from 2013 have a lower average LTV at origination (84% against 92%) and a lower interest-only share (11% against 49% of the balance), and their 12-month arrears incidence is lower in every loan-age band. Collections were centralised in 2016 with an earlier first contact (day 5 instead of day 15 of arrears); cure rates from 30 days past due rose from 58% to 67%, which is captured by the arrears-history risk drivers rather than by a break in the default rate series. No change in Dutch insolvency or foreclosure law with an effect on the default definition occurred in the observation period; debt restructuring under the WSNP procedure is captured as a bankruptcy trigger throughout.

sections.heading: Economic conditions in the observation period
sections.text: The observation period covers the end of the Dutch housing market correction (house prices fell by 6.3% in 2012 and 6.6% in 2013 before recovering from mid-2013), the peak in unemployment of 7.4% in 2014, the expansion of 2015–2019, the COVID-19 period with temporary payment deferrals for 1,870 facilities in 2020, and the interest-rate increases of 2022–2023 with the temporary house-price decline of 2023. Current and foreseeable conditions (high house prices, low unemployment and mortgage rates above the 2015–2021 level) are within the range observed in the RDS; the interest-rate level of 2023–2024 was last observed in 2012. The effect of the payment deferrals of 2020 on the default rate series is assessed in the model development document.

sections.heading: DQ rules and thresholds
sections.text: The DQ rules for the 49 critical data elements (38 candidate variables and 11 default-flag components) were defined jointly by the model developers and the Data Stewards; 212 rules are documented in Annex A and 164 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool. Each rule has an amber and a red threshold equal to or stricter than the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3: completeness below 98% and 95% non-missing, reconciliation differences above 0.5% and 1% of the amount, and consistency below 99% and 98% of records passing. For the target variable and its constituents the thresholds are stricter: 100% completeness of the default flag and default date, and a red threshold of 0.1% for unmatched default events in the reconciliation to the default register. No threshold less strict than the default was applied, so no deviation required approval under MRM-STD-022 §4.5. Data quality of the RDS is managed in accordance with MRM-STD-022, and all DQ results are produced by versioned code from the frozen RDS.

sections.heading: DQ results per dimension
sections.text: Record-level completeness was confirmed by comparing the number of facilities, obligors and default events per snapshot with the mortgage administration system and the default register, and attribute-level completeness is at least 99.4% for all critical data elements except debt-to-income at origination (97.7%, amber, see §4.3). Accuracy was measured by reconciling outstanding balances to the general ledger at each year-end (maximum difference 0.08%) and default events to the default register (§6.6), and by the sample-based verification in §6.5. Consistency was checked between the three source systems, between related fields (for example origination date before snapshot date, arrears amount not exceeding the outstanding balance) and over the observation period, including the change of the default definition in 2016; 99.7% of records pass all logical consistency rules. Validity (permitted values and ranges) and uniqueness (one record per facility and snapshot) are met for 100% of records after the build, and appropriateness for the range of application is assessed in chapter 5. The DQ assessment report in Annex D lists the result of each rule per variable and dimension against its thresholds, and the number and share of records excluded per exclusion reason. The gaps identified, namely the amber completeness of debt-to-income at origination and the approximated default flag before 2016, are explained in §4.3 and §6.2, and their effect on the reliability of the estimates is assessed in the data deficiency log (§6.7).

sections.heading: Sample-based verification and collateral data
sections.text: As required for Tier 1 models, a random sample of 400 facilities was verified against the credit files and valuation reports in the document management system; the accuracy of LTV at origination, income at origination and valuation date was 99.0%, 98.5% and 99.5% respectively, and the 12 deviations found were corrected at source by Mortgage Operations. Collateral data (type, value, valuation date and method, lien rank and link to the secured facilities) are held in the collateral valuation database and meet the completeness and consistency thresholds of MRM-STD-022 for all snapshots after the migration of June 2019; for earlier snapshots the valuation method is missing for 3.1% of collateral records, which does not affect the indexed LTV. Residential properties are valued independently at origination, indexed quarterly with the regional price index and revalued at least every three years or upon a credit event, in accordance with CR-POL-001 §8.3. The house-price index and the automated valuations were compared with 2,450 full valuations obtained in 2023–2024; the median absolute deviation of the indexed value is 6.8%, with no systematic bias by province.

sections.heading: Reconciliation of the default flag and key amounts
sections.text: For default events from January 2021 the RDS default flag was reconciled to the default register maintained under CR-STD-110: 2,146 of 2,151 obligor-level default events match on obligor and default date, and the five differences are technical past due cases corrected in the register after the source extraction and removed from the RDS. IRB and IFRS 9 default flags are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems by Credit Risk Reporting, and the reconciliations for 2021–2024 show no difference in the obligors flagged as defaulted. Outstanding balances and record counts per reference date were reconciled to the general ledger and to the COREP exposure data at each year-end; differences are below 0.1% of the balance and are explained by accrued interest booked on separate accounts. Default status is recorded at obligor level in the arrears management system and propagated daily to the mortgage administration system and the risk data warehouse, so that all facilities of a defaulted obligor carry the default flag in all systems from the same date.

sections.heading: Data deficiency log
sections.text: The data deficiency log of PD-MORT-NL v4, maintained under MRM-STD-022 §7, contains five entries: DD-01 approximated default flag 2012–2015 (see §6.2); DD-02 missing debt-to-income at origination (2.3% of facilities, mainly loans originated before 2014); DD-03 facilities excluded for incomplete collateral information; DD-04 missing valuation method before the collateral database migration of June 2019; DD-05 origination data unavailable for the former brand portfolio. Each entry records the affected variables and segments, the DQ dimension, the cause, the estimated impact and the treatment (approximation, imputation, exclusion or no action), and is cross-referenced to the limitations log in chapter 8 of the model development document (LIM-01 to LIM-04). DD-02 to DD-05 are also recorded in the Bank data issue register (DI-2026-0318 to DI-2026-0321) with an owner, a remediation plan and a target date: DD-02 and DD-04 are remediated at source by Mortgage Operations with target date 31 December 2027, whereas DD-03 and DD-05 cannot be remediated at source because the historical data no longer exist.

sections.heading: Personal data attributes, lawful basis and purpose limitation
sections.text: The RDS contains 19 personal data attributes of natural persons, listed in Annex A with their purpose in the model, the lawful basis, the pseudonymisation applied and the retention period. An attribute is retained only where it is a candidate risk driver or is needed to construct the default flag or the observation structure; of 31 attributes initially requested, 12 were removed in the data minimisation review of 4 November 2026 (among others marital status, number of children and employer name). Processing for model development, validation and application is based on Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR, as it is necessary for compliance with the Bank's legal obligations under CRR Articles 144, 179 and 180, and this lawful basis was recorded before processing started. The data were originally collected for the conclusion and administration of mortgage contracts, and the compatibility of their reuse for IRB modelling was assessed under Art. 6(4) GDPR in the DPIA, considering the link between the purposes, the context of collection, the nature of the data, the possible consequences for data subjects and the pseudonymisation applied. The processing is recorded in the Record of Processing as RoP-RISK-0231 with its purposes, data categories, recipients, absence of transfers and retention periods, and the model inventory record of MDL-01 references this entry.

sections.heading: Pseudonymisation, security, transfers and retention
sections.text: The RDS is pseudonymised: customer and facility numbers are replaced by keyed tokens generated by the Data Protection Services team, which holds the keys separately from the modelling environment. Re-identification requires a request to Data Protection Services for a documented purpose approved by the Privacy Office and is logged; one request (the file verification of §6.5) was approved on 2 February 2027. The RDS is held in the approved secure analytics environment of the Risk function with role-based access restricted to 14 named staff of Retail Credit Risk Modelling and Model Validation – Credit Risk, logging of all access and encryption at rest. Test environments of the production implementation use masked data derived from the RDS; no production personal data are copied to test environments. All processing takes place in the Bank's data centres in the Netherlands, and no personal data are transferred outside the EEA or to third-party AI services. Personal data in the RDS and development snapshots are retained for the period of use of PD-MORT-NL v4 plus five years after its decommissioning; thereafter they are deleted or irreversibly anonymised and the deletion is evidenced in the retention log of the analytics platform, and the monthly staging snapshots not retained in the RDS are deleted six months after the RDS freeze.

sections.heading: Data protection impact assessment
sections.text: DPIA-2026-118 was completed on 18 December 2026 for PD-MORT-NL v4, as required for Tier 1 models and for models that score natural persons for decisions; it describes the processing and its purposes, assesses necessity and proportionality, identifies the risks to data subjects (among others incorrect prioritisation in arrears management and indirect discrimination through proxy variables) and sets out the mitigating measures. The Data Protection Officer advised on 11 December 2026 that the residual risk is not high after the measures, so prior consultation of the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens was not required. DPIA-2026-118 replaces DPIA-2021-047 for PD-MORT-NL v3 because v4 introduces new personal data attributes (income type and payment reminders); it is reviewed at every material change and at the latest in December 2029. The DPIA, the Record of Processing entry and the minimisation review together document how the Bank demonstrates compliance with the Art. 5(1) GDPR principles in the development, validation and application of the model.

sections.heading: Protected attributes and proxy screening
sections.text: Nationality, gender, ethnicity, religion and health data are not included in the RDS, and no special categories of personal data under Art. 9(1) GDPR are processed. Borrower age is retained only for proxy screening and outcome testing and was not offered as a candidate risk driver, because its use was not approved by Credit Risk Management under CR-POL-001 §9.2. Proxy screening measured the association of each candidate variable with gender (taken from a separate access-restricted extract that is not part of the RDS) and with age band using Cramér's V; only postcode exceeded the screening threshold of 0.15 (V = 0.19 with age band), and it is therefore used solely at provincial level within the house-price index, which is the minimum aggregation needed for collateral indexation. The results of the proxy screening are documented in Annex B.5 of this document, and the outcome testing of the final model is documented in section 7.5 of the model development document.

sections.heading: Build environment, rebuild result and access for validation
sections.text: Tag v4.0.0 of repository rds-mort-nl (commit 7c41e2a of 24 February 2027) produced the frozen RDS RDS-MORT-NL-v4.0 from source snapshots with reference date 31 December 2025, extracted from the risk data warehouse on 15 January 2027. The software environment is Python 3.11.7 with pandas 2.1.4 and pyarrow 14.0.2 on analytics platform image rca-py311-2026.4, and the random seed of the sampling in §2.3 is fixed in the build configuration. A full rebuild on 5 June 2027 from the tagged code and the archived source snapshots reproduced 9,600,412 rows and 43,118 default observations, identical to the frozen RDS. The build code was reviewed before the RDS freeze by a second developer who did not write it (S. Visser, review record RCRM-1519 of 23 February 2027). This document, Annex A and the build code README describe every extraction, filter, exclusion, default-flag and derivation step in enough detail for Model Validation to rebuild the RDS independently from the source snapshots, to which Model Validation has direct read access in the risk data warehouse. The build code, source snapshots and frozen RDS remain available and the RDS remains reproducible throughout the validation and the supervisory assessment of the application.

sections.heading: Purpose and regulatory use
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL v4 estimates the 12-month probability of default of Dutch residential mortgage obligors for the calculation of own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach (CRR Articles 143 and 180) and replaces PD-MORT-NL v3, approved by the ECB in 2022. The model assigns every obligor in the range of application to one of the 12 non-defaulted grades of the retail master scale, and the grade PD is used in the own funds calculation, in credit risk appetite metrics (expected loss, RWA density and grade distribution of the mortgage book), in risk-adjusted pricing of the mortgage offer, in internal capital allocation to Retail Banking and in management reporting. The secondary use is the prioritisation of arrears management: Retail Collections uses the monthly grade to set contact intensity for obligors in S2, and the early-warning monitoring of CR-POL-001 §10.1 uses a downgrade of three or more grades as an early-warning indicator for review within 30 days. Credit decisions on new mortgages and on restructuring or renewal of existing mortgages require a valid grade from the approved rating system: new applications are graded with the application variant of the scorecard at origination, and existing obligors receive their monthly behavioural grade from PD-MORT-NL. The model is used only within the range of application in §1.2.

sections.heading: Range of application
sections.text: The range of application comprises all owner-occupied residential mortgage loans to natural persons in the Netherlands in the retail exposure class secured by immovable property, including the migrated former brand portfolio; at 31 December 2026 it contained 376,900 facilities of 164,300 obligors with an EAD of EUR 37.4 billion and RWEA of EUR 4,436 million under v3. Buy-to-let mortgages, mortgages to legal entities and commercial real estate are outside the range of application and are rated by other rating systems; the assignment to the retail exposure class and to this rating system follows the exposure class methodology and is performed automatically in the credit risk engine. The IRB approach is applied to all exposures of the retail mortgage exposure type, and no exposures in the range of application are under permanent partial use of the Standardised Approach. Extensions of the range of application to new products or obligor types are assessed under MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 before use, including the demonstration of representativeness and comparability.

sections.heading: Users and parameters used for internal purposes
sections.text: The main users are Credit Risk Reporting (own funds calculation), Retail Credit Risk Management (risk appetite and portfolio steering), Retail Collections (arrears management), Finance (capital allocation) and Mortgage Pricing. The IFRS 9 ECL model for residential mortgages (MDL-07) does not use the IRB PD directly but uses the PD-MORT-NL v4 grade as an input; where IRB PDs are used for purposes that require unbiased estimates, the MoC and the regulatory floor are removed and the removal is documented in the user guide. Pricing uses the grade PD including MoC, identical to the own funds parameter, so no difference arises between internal and regulatory parameters for that use. The known limitations of chapter 8 and the conditions attached to the approval are communicated to users in the PD-MORT-NL v4 user guide and in the credit risk manual for Retail Collections. The grade is not used for any decision based solely on automated processing: arrears management actions are taken by collection officers who see the main drivers of the grade and may deviate from the suggested contact strategy, so Art. 22 GDPR does not apply to the use of the model.

sections.heading: Tier, materiality and complexity
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL is a Tier 1 model: materiality is High on exposure and own funds impact (the largest retail IRB portfolio of the Bank) and complexity is Medium (statistical model with two segments, approximated historical default data and several expert judgements), which leads to Tier 1 in the materiality-by-complexity matrix of MRM-STD-010 §6.4. The tier was proposed by the model owner with the tiering template, approved by Model Risk Management on 22 September 2026 and will be confirmed at the initial validation; it exceeds the minimum Tier 2 for models used for own funds requirements. The tier is reviewed at least annually and at every material change; the last review on 15 March 2027 confirmed Tier 1. The complexity assessment under the ECB guide classifies the model as not highly complex (no machine-learning technique, no dynamic recalibration), and the rating system is classified as material in the Bank's IRB materiality assessment communicated to the ECB in the annual IRB roll-out and materiality report. As a Tier 1 IRB model, PD-MORT-NL v4 is validated before first use, annually thereafter and in full scope at least every three years.

sections.heading: Model inventory, ownership and AI Act assessment
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL is registered in the model inventory under identifier MDL-01; version 4.0 was registered at gate G0 on 22 September 2026, before development started, after the model identification questionnaire had confirmed that the method is a model under MRM-POL-001 §3. The model owner is E. van Dijk (Head of Retail Credit Risk Modelling), the developers are M. Bakker and S. Visser, and the assigned validation team is Model Validation – Credit Risk; the model owner remains accountable for use within the approved scope, the inventory record, monitoring, remediation of findings and fulfilment of approval conditions. The inventory record states the model name, version, purpose, intended and secondary uses, range of application, risk type, regulatory use, model family, tier with scores, lifecycle stage and gate status, the latest validation opinion on v3, open findings, limitations, the supervisory permission status and the DPIA reference DPIA-2026-118; the model owner updates it within ten business days of any change and attests it quarterly. Before gate G1 the inventory records that PD-MORT-NL v4 is not an AI system within Art. 3(1) of the AI Act: it is a logistic regression with fixed, documented coefficients estimated once with standard statistical methods, which falls under the exclusion for simple prediction systems in the Commission guidelines on the AI system definition, and it is not used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons for access to credit. The model is developed internally and is managed under the Model Risk Management Policy; no vendor or group entity is involved in its design, data or operation.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The rating system consists of six separated components in line with CRM-STD-100 §4.3: (a) two segment-specific logistic regression scorecards (risk differentiation); (b) the assignment of scores to the 12 grades of the retail master scale; (c) the calibration of grade PDs to the long-run average default rate per calibration segment; (d) the margin of conservatism; (e) the regulatory PD floor; and (f) the override process. The risk differentiation step (chapter 4) and the risk quantification step (chapters 5 and 6) are developed, documented and tested separately, and both meet CRR Art. 179 and CRM-STD-100. Obligors are assigned to grades on the basis of obligor characteristics (income type, debt-service-to-income at origination, arrears and payment behaviour), transaction characteristics (interest-only share, loan age, NHG guarantee, indexed loan-to-value of the collateral) and delinquency (days past due, arrears history and forbearance). PD is assigned at obligor level: property-related drivers are computed over all loan parts secured by the same property, arrears drivers over all facilities of the obligor, and all facilities of an obligor receive the same grade.

sections.heading: Segmentation and rating philosophy
sections.text: The population is split into two segments that are also the calibration segments: S1 comprises obligors without any day past due above the materiality threshold in the previous 12 months (98.6% of observations, long-run average default rate 0.29%), and S2 obligors with at least one such day in the previous 12 months (1.4% of observations, long-run average default rate 11.2%). The segmentation is an expert judgement in model design (EJ-PDM4-02), supported by the finding that arrears variables dominate the risk ranking in S2 while they carry no information in S1, and by a single-model alternative that has an out-of-time Gini of 0.771 against 0.789 for the segmented model. Separate scorecards per segment lead to grades with homogeneous risk: within S1 the ranking is driven by collateral and affordability, within S2 by the severity and recency of arrears. PD-MORT-NL v4 follows the Bank's hybrid rating philosophy of CRM-STD-100 §4.2: grade assignment responds to current conditions through indexed LTV (house prices) and payment behaviour, while the PD per grade is calibrated to the long-run average default rate. In a downturn obligors are expected to migrate to worse grades while grade-level default rates remain broadly stable; over 2012–2024 the share of obligors in grades R07–R12 fell from 6.9% (2013) to 3.1% (2024), while the yearly default rate of each grade stayed within ±30% of its long-run average, which is consistent with the chosen philosophy. The rating philosophy, including the assumptions on net migration across grades, is unchanged from PD-MORT-NL v3.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and processes
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL v4 uses the output of the collateral indexation process (regional CBS/Kadaster index) and of the automated valuation model for the indexed LTV, and it provides grades and PDs to LGD-MORT-NL (expected loss best estimate), to the IFRS 9 mortgage model (MDL-07) and to the ICAAP credit risk stress test. In the ICAAP and EBA stress tests the grade distribution is projected under the severe but plausible recession scenarios of the Bank by shocking house prices and unemployment, and the resulting rating migration and effect on own funds requirements are reported to the Asset and Liability Committee; in the 2026 ICAAP adverse scenario the average PD of the portfolio increased by a factor of 2.4. The stress-test projection uses a satellite model that approximates grade migration from house-price and unemployment shocks; this approximation, its back-test on 2012–2014 and its limitations are documented in the stress-test methodology and referenced in the stress-test reports.

sections.heading: Changes relative to PD-MORT-NL v3
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL v4 changes the rating system as follows: the observation period is extended from 2012–2019 to 2012–2024; the single scorecard of v3 is replaced by two segment scorecards; five risk drivers are new (interest-only share, loan age, self-employed income type, payment reminders and months since last cure) and three v3 drivers are removed (original LTV, borrower age band and product type); and the MoC is re-quantified under CRM-STD-101 v2.0. Rank ordering changes significantly: the Spearman rank correlation between v3 and v4 scores on the December 2026 portfolio is 0.86, below the significance level of 0.90 defined in the Bank's change policy, and 34.6% of exposures change grade. The master scale, the definition of default, the override policy and the rating philosophy are unchanged. The classification of the change is documented in the model change memorandum CHG-2026-0417.

sections.heading: Reference data set
sections.text: Development and calibration use the frozen RDS RDS-MORT-NL-v4.0, documented in the approved RDS documentation (Dataset Construction and DQ Assessment – Residential Real Estate Mortgages, version 1.0): 9,600,412 account-months of 780,000 facilities from monthly snapshots January 2012 to December 2024, with 43,118 observations followed by a default within 12 months. The RDS draws on internal data only: the mortgage administration system, the arrears management system and the collateral valuation database, complemented by the regional house-price index for collateral indexation. All relevant and current information available for the portfolio is used in the grade assignment: the monthly snapshot of contract, collateral and arrears data is complete for 99.4% of the critical data elements, and debt-to-income at origination is imputed conservatively where missing.

sections.heading: Development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples
sections.text: The samples were defined in the development plan before estimation: observations from January 2012 to December 2022 were split at obligor level into a development sample (70%: 5,684,210 observations, 27,075 defaults) and an out-of-sample holdout (30%: 2,436,090 observations, 11,603 defaults), and all observations from January 2023 to December 2024 form the out-of-time sample (1,480,112 observations, 4,440 defaults). The out-of-time sample was not used for variable selection or parameter estimation; it was used only for performance testing and for the calibration tests in §5.4. Observations are weighted by the inverse of the number of facilities of the obligor in the snapshot, so that obligors with several loan parts are not overweighted. Default rates are 0.48% in the development and out-of-sample data and 0.30% in the out-of-time sample, reflecting the benign conditions of 2023–2024.

sections.heading: Definition of default and data deficiencies
sections.text: The target is the default of the obligor under CR-STD-110 within 12 months after the snapshot; the definitions of default and the historical approximations are documented in RDS §3.2–3.8, and their consistency with CRR Art. 178 is demonstrated in the Definition of Default implementation memo. The same default events are used for PD-MORT-NL v4 and LGD-MORT-NL. Because the RDS combines three default-definition regimes (approximated 2012–2015, re-derived 2016–2020 and register-based from 2021), their effect on the estimates is reflected by segment-specific tests and by the category A MoC in chapter 6. Risk differentiation under the current definition is demonstrated on the time series 2021–2024 of realised default rates per grade, which is based entirely on the default register under CR-STD-110 v2.0: the out-of-time Gini on 2023–2024 is 0.789 and the Gini on the 2021–2022 out-of-sample observations is 0.796. The five data deficiencies of RDS §6.7 are treated as follows: DD-01 (approximated default flag 2012–2015) is covered by MoC A1; DD-02 (imputed debt-to-income at origination) by MoC A2; DD-03 and DD-05 (exclusions) by the appropriate adjustment AA-01 and MoC A3; DD-04 (missing valuation method before 2019) has no effect on the model variables and requires no treatment. Each deficiency is recorded in the limitations log (LIM-01 to LIM-04) and in the MoC register with a reference to the data deficiency log entry. The expert judgement applied in the treatment of DD-02 (imputation with the segment median, EJ-PDM4-03 for the related LTV capping) is linked to the assessment of MoC A2 in §6.2.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives
sections.text: Four alternatives were assessed against the criteria of MRM-STD-020 §6.1 (regulatory requirements, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation): (1) segmented logistic regression scorecards; (2) a gradient boosting model (LightGBM); (3) a discrete-time hazard model; and (4) the v3 single scorecard re-estimated on the new RDS. Out-of-time Gini coefficients were 0.789, 0.801, 0.781 and 0.763 respectively; the gradient boosting model performs slightly better but is less transparent, less stable over time (PSI of the score 0.12 against 0.07) and would require the explainability controls of AI-STD-700, while the hazard model offers no gain for a 12-month horizon. The segmented logistic regression is selected because it is conceptually sound for a 12-month default horizon, consistent with the pool-based treatment of retail exposures, fully interpretable at driver level and implementable in the existing rating engine; the performance difference with the gradient boosting model (0.012 Gini) is not considered material. The logistic regression models the log-odds of default within 12 months as a linear function of weight-of-evidence transformed risk drivers, estimated by weighted maximum likelihood; its assumptions (independence of observations conditional on the drivers, linearity in the weight-of-evidence scale, stability of driver effects over time) are tested in §4.4 and chapter 7.

sections.heading: Long list of candidate risk drivers
sections.text: The long list of 38 candidate drivers combines the drivers of v3, variables proposed in two expert workshops with Retail Credit Risk Management and Retail Collections (28 October and 4 November 2026) and new data available since 2019; it covers collateral, affordability, product, payment behaviour, arrears history and forbearance. For each candidate the expected direction of the effect on PD was recorded before estimation (for example positive for indexed LTV, interest-only share and payment reminders, negative for months since last cure), together with its economic rationale, availability at the point of use in the monthly production run and stability over the observation period. Climate-related and environmental risk drivers were assessed: the energy label of the property (available for 81% of facilities) and a flood-risk indicator for the location showed no significant additional explanatory power after controlling for indexed LTV (p-values 0.21 and 0.47), so they are not included; their materiality is reassessed in each annual review. Credit bureau data (BKR) are used only at origination and are not model inputs, so no adjustment for outdated bureau or financial statement information is needed. Borrower age, gender and nationality were not offered as candidates, in line with CR-POL-001 §9 and the proxy screening of RDS §7.4.

sections.heading: Univariate analysis and seasoning
sections.text: Each candidate was binned (at most eight bins, minimum 5% of observations per bin, monotone weight of evidence unless economically justified) and assessed on the development sample for information value, univariate Gini, the stability of its weight of evidence across the calendar years 2012–2022 and the share of missing values. Candidates with an information value below 0.02, with a sign of the weight of evidence contradicting the expected direction, or with a PSI above 0.10 between 2012–2016 and 2017–2022 were removed; 24 of the 38 candidates passed this step. The non-monotone relation of loan age with default risk (a peak between 24 and 60 months after origination) was kept because it reflects the seasoning pattern described below. Seasoning was analysed by origination cohort: 12-month default rates rise during the first two years after origination, peak between 24 and 60 months and decline thereafter, and this pattern is stable across the cohorts 2012–2020. Loan age is included as a risk driver in S1, so the expected change of the PD over the life of the exposure is reflected in the grade assignment; in S2 loan age has no additional explanatory power once arrears are known. Interest-only loans originated before 2013 reach contractual maturity from 2030 onwards; because the RDS contains no maturities of such loans, the refinancing risk at maturity is recorded as limitation LIM-05.

sections.heading: Multivariate selection and final model
sections.text: Among pairs of candidates with a Spearman correlation above 0.6 the candidate with the higher information value was kept, and stepwise selection per segment (entry at p < 0.01, retention at p < 0.001) was followed by an expert review of the selected set, which forced the NHG flag into S1 (EJ-PDM4-04); the variance inflation factors of the final drivers are below 1.9. The final S1 scorecard contains seven drivers (indexed LTV, interest-only share, loan age, NHG guarantee, debt-service-to-income at origination, self-employed income type and number of payment reminders in the last 24 months), and the final S2 scorecard contains six drivers (current days-past-due bucket, maximum days past due in the last 12 months, months since last cure, indexed LTV, arrears amount relative to the monthly instalment and forbearance in the last 24 months). All coefficients on the weight-of-evidence scale are positive and significant at 0.1%, which confirms the expected direction of every driver, and their magnitudes are plausible (for example, an increase of indexed LTV from 60–80% to above 100% raises the odds of default in S1 by a factor of 2.7). The drivers form a reasonable and effective basis for the prediction, cover the material drivers identified in the expert workshops, show no material bias across regions, product types or origination cohorts, and do not distort own funds requirements.

sections.heading: Final scorecards and replication
sections.text: The scorecard points are scaled to 600 points at odds of 50:1 with 20 points to double the odds, and the full specification (bins, weights of evidence, coefficients, points per bin and score cut-offs per grade) is given in Annex 4 and in parameter file pd_mort_nl_v4_params.json of tag v4.0.3. The grade assignment is fully determined by the scorecards and the cut-offs, so Model Validation and other third parties can replicate the assignment of every observation from the RDS and the parameter file, and the rating criteria are applied identically for all distribution channels, regions and business units. All drivers are measured at the monthly snapshot date and relate to the same 12-month horizon in development, calibration and application. Production computes the score monthly from the same fields and transformations, as specified in the implementation specification.
