sections.heading: Treatment of missing values and outliers in estimation
sections.text: Missing values are classified per variable: debt-to-income at origination is missing because of a data deficiency (2.3%, DD-02) and is imputed with the segment median of the origination year; months since last cure is structurally missing for obligors that never had arrears and is assigned its own bin; no other driver has missing values above 0.1%. The imputation is performed by the build code and is reproducible; re-estimating the S1 scorecard with a regression imputation instead of the segment median changes the average PD by +0.3% and the Gini by less than 0.001, and the residual uncertainty is covered by MoC A2. Indexed LTV is capped at 250% (EJ-PDM4-03), which affects 0.02% of observations, all in the highest LTV bin; the cap is applied identically in development and production, and caps at 200% or 300% leave the Gini and the grade distribution unchanged.

sections.heading: Calibration target, long-run average and calibration sample
sections.text: Grade PDs are calibrated per calibration segment to the long-run average of one-year default rates, defined as the arithmetic average of the one-year default rates at the 52 quarter-end reference dates from March 2012 to December 2024 computed with overlapping one-year windows as described in RDS §2.5. The long-run average default rate is 0.44% for the portfolio, 0.29% for S1 and 11.2% for S2, after the appropriate adjustment AA-01 for the exclusions (+0.01 percentage points on the portfolio level). Overlapping quarterly windows were chosen after analysing the alternatives: the long-run average based on non-overlapping January windows differs by 0.006 percentage points, seasonality of defaults within the year is not significant, and short-term contracts do not occur in the portfolio. The calibration is consistent with the definition of default used for the target variable. The calibration sample of each calibration segment consists of all obligors in the range of application at the 52 quarter-end reference dates from March 2012 to December 2024 (8.37 million obligor-dates, of which 116,200 in S2), scored with the final scorecards. The calibration sample is stored read-only as RDS-MORT-NL-v4.0-CAL next to the frozen RDS, and its construction is part of tag v4.0.0 of the build code. Obligors that change segment between reference dates are included in the segment in which they are at the reference date.

sections.heading: Representativeness of the long-run average period
sections.text: The observation period includes the most recent five years and all earlier years with facility-level data, and it contains the 2012–2014 downturn with the highest default rates of the available history. The period is therefore considered to reflect the likely range of variability of default rates, and no upward adjustment of the long-run average is applied; no adjustment lowers the long-run average below the observed average. Facility-level data before 2012 are not available, so the long-run average cannot be compared with the reference period 2008–2018; the aggregate annual 90-days arrears rates of the predecessor system for 2009–2011 (0.52% to 0.71%) are below the 2012–2013 default rates, which indicates that the observation period is not less severe than the years preceding it. The long-run average of v4 (0.44%) is lower than that of v3 (0.54% over 2012–2019) because the extended window adds the five benign years 2020–2024, which shows that the estimates reflect the new data that have become available since the last development.

sections.heading: Calibration method, grade assignment and PD floor
sections.text: Calibration is performed per calibration segment by shifting the intercept of the scorecard so that the average calibrated PD over the calibration sample equals the segment long-run average; the shift preserves the rank ordering of obligors within the segment. Each obligor is then assigned to the grade of the retail master scale (R01–R12, with RD for defaulted obligors) whose PD boundaries of CRM-STD-100 §5.2 contain its calibrated PD, and the grade PD is the average calibrated PD of the grade in the calibration sample; continuous PDs are not used in the own funds calculation. Grade PDs before MoC are R01 0.06%, R02 0.14%, R03 0.27%, R04 0.46%, R05 0.78%, R06 1.33%, R07 2.28%, R08 4.05%, R09 7.30%, R10 13.9%, R11 25.8% and R12 47.5%; each grade maps to exactly one master scale grade and PDs increase monotonically with grade. Calibration is performed after overrides are taken into account (overridden obligors enter with their final grade) and before the application of the MoC and the regulatory PD floor. Grade assignments are refreshed monthly in production and therefore at least annually for every obligor. The PD applied to each exposure is floored at 0.05% in accordance with CRR Art. 163(1) and CRM-STD-100 §11.1, after the MoC; the lowest final grade PD is 0.07% (R01), so the floor is not binding for any grade. The floor is applied at exposure level in the production engine, and the share of exposures and EAD for which it is binding (0% at 31 December 2026) is reported in the quarterly monitoring report.

sections.heading: Calibration tests
sections.text: For each of the 52 reference dates the average best-estimate PD per calibration segment was compared with the one-year default rate and with the long-run average default rate: in S1 the average PD ranges from 0.25% to 0.36% against one-year default rates of 0.12% to 0.58%, and in S2 from 10.1% to 12.6% against 7.9% to 15.8%, a pattern consistent with a hybrid rating philosophy. Per grade, the Jeffreys test of the best-estimate PD against the default rate over the full calibration sample shows no grade with p < 5%, and the long-run default rate of every grade lies within ±12% of its grade PD. Qualitative calibration analyses confirm a unimodal distribution of obligors over the grades, a minimum of 1,100 obligors per grade at every reference date after 2014 and no excessive concentration (§5.5). Calibration test results on the out-of-time sample are reported in §7.2.

sections.heading: Grade distribution, homogeneity and concentration
sections.text: At 31 December 2026 the largest grade, R02, contains 28.4% of the exposures of the rating system, below the 30% limit of CRM-STD-100 §5.4, and the number-weighted Herfindahl index of the grade distribution is 0.19. Homogeneity within grades was tested by comparing the default rate of subsets defined by NHG, interest-only share, origination cohort, region and self-employed status with the rest of the grade (chi-square test at 5%); 3 of 96 tests are significant, which is within the number expected by chance, and no material subset shows a significantly different default rate. Heterogeneity between adjacent grades was tested with one-sided z-tests on the long-run default rates: all adjacent pairs differ significantly at 1% except R11 and R12 (p = 0.032), which are kept separate because of the large difference in PD (25.8% against 47.5%) and the small number of obligors in R12. The number of exposures in each grade is sufficient for meaningful quantification and validation, with at least 1,100 obligors and 60 default events per grade over the observation period.

sections.heading: Identification of deficiencies and appropriate adjustments
sections.text: Deficiencies were identified systematically with the trigger list of Annex 1 of CRM-STD-101, covering RDS completeness, the definition of default, methods, systems and processes, underwriting and policies, the environment and the estimation error. Five deficiencies were identified, and each was assigned to exactly one category and recorded in the MoC register: category A – A1 approximated default flag 2012–2015, A2 imputation of debt-to-income at origination, A3 exclusions; category B – B1 changes in underwriting standards 2013–2018, B2 payment deferrals and support measures in 2020–2021; the general estimation error is covered by category C per segment. Three triggers were considered and rejected: the migration of the collateral database in 2019 (no effect on model variables), the centralisation of collections in 2016 (captured by the arrears drivers, no break in default rates) and the low number of defaults (not applicable, all segments have more than 14,000 default observations). The deficiencies raised in the validation of v3 (V3-F01 on the calibration of the arrears segment and V3-F02 on self-employed obligors) were assessed and are addressed by the segmentation and by the self-employed risk driver, so no MoC component was added for them. For each deficiency an appropriate adjustment was considered first: for A3 the long-run average is increased by 0.01 percentage points (adjustment AA-01), which neutralises the effect of the exclusions quantified in RDS §4.2, and the remaining uncertainty of the adjustment is covered by MoC A3. For A1 no appropriate adjustment is applied because the undercount of default events in 2012–2015 cannot be estimated reliably year by year; the effect is covered in full by MoC A1. For B1 and B2 no adjustment is possible because the counterfactual default rates are not observable; the adjusted long-run average of 0.44% is the best estimate of the portfolio default rate over the cycle.

sections.heading: Category A MoC
sections.text: MoC A1 (+6.0%) covers the approximated default flag for 2012–2015: applying the approximation rule of RDS §3.2 to the 2016 data, for which the CR-STD-110 components are available, yields 5.7% fewer default events than the flag under the current definition, and the MoC is set at +6% relative on the long-run average of both segments. MoC A2 (+0.5%) covers the imputation of debt-to-income at origination, based on the sensitivity to the alternative imputation method in §4.6 (+0.3%) rounded up. MoC A3 (+0.5%) covers the uncertainty of adjustment AA-01, based on the range of default rates of the excluded facilities (0.41% to 0.53% at a 90% confidence level). Category A MoC is quantified per calibration segment and totals +7.0% in S1 and S2; it covers both the uncertainty from the appropriate adjustment and the uncorrected deficiencies, and each component is non-negative.

sections.heading: Category B and category C MoC
sections.text: MoC B1 (+2.0% in both segments) covers the changes in underwriting standards between 2013 and 2018 (reduction of the LTV limit and the amortisation requirement), which lower the default risk of recent cohorts in a way that the long-run average of older cohorts does not reflect fully; it is quantified by comparing the long-run average with and without the cohorts originated before 2013. MoC B2 (+1.5% in S1, +1.0% in S2) covers the payment deferrals and government support of 2020–2021, which may have suppressed default rates in those years; it is based on expert judgement (EJ-PDM4-06) because neither re-estimation nor benchmarking can reproduce the counterfactual default rates, and it was approved by the model owner and the head of the modelling unit. Category B MoC totals +3.5% in S1 and +3.0% in S2. MoC C covers the general estimation error of the long-run average and is derived from the one-sided 90% upper confidence bound of the long-run average per segment. The bootstrap design (block length and number of replications) and the resulting values per segment are being finalised and will be added in the next version.

sections.heading: Aggregation and application of the MoC
sections.text: The total MoC per calibration segment is the simple sum of the category A, B and C components without diversification: +19.5% in S1 and +16.1% in S2, equivalent to +18.3% on the portfolio long-run average. So that each grade has a single final PD, the MoC of a grade is the average of the segment MoCs weighted by the share of each segment in that grade in the calibration sample: +19.5% for R01–R06, decreasing to +16.1% for R12. The final PD of each grade is its best estimate plus the MoC and is then subject to the regulatory floor: final grade PDs are R01 0.07%, R02 0.17%, R03 0.32%, R04 0.55%, R05 0.93%, R06 1.59%, R07 2.71%, R08 4.80%, R09 8.58%, R10 16.3%, R11 30.1% and R12 55.1%. Because the grade add-ons decrease only gradually from 19.5% to 16.1% while best-estimate PDs increase by at least 70% from one grade to the next, the MoC preserves the rank ordering and final PDs increase monotonically with grade and remain within the boundaries of their master scale grade. The total MoC is below 20% of the best estimate, so the redevelopment trigger of CRM-STD-101 §7.2 is not met, and the MoC is quantified in accordance with paragraphs 36–52 of EBA/GL/2017/16.

sections.heading: MoC register, reporting and remediation
sections.text: The MoC register of PD-MORT-NL v4 records for each deficiency the category, the affected components and calibration segments, the quantification method, the MoC value, the related data deficiency log entry and the remediation status, and this chapter together with the register constitutes the list of all identified deficiencies required in the model documentation. Every category A deficiency has a remediation plan with owner and target date or is documented as permanent: A1 and A3 are permanent (historical data no longer exist) and are reassessed at each annual review, and A2 is remediated at source by 31 December 2027. MoC levels are monitored in the annual review of estimates and reported internally separately for categories A, B and C; the effect of the MoC on RWEA at 31 December 2026 is EUR 212 million (A EUR 81 million, B EUR 41 million, C EUR 90 million). An MoC component is reduced or removed only after the underlying deficiency has been remediated and Model Validation has confirmed the remediation, and any change of the MoC is processed as a model change under MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power and stability
sections.text: Discriminatory power was measured on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples for the whole model and per segment: the Gini coefficient is 0.812, 0.806 and 0.789 for the whole model (out-of-time 95% DeLong interval 0.776–0.802), 0.662, 0.655 and 0.641 for S1, and 0.583, 0.577 and 0.561 for S2. All values are above the thresholds of MV-HB-003 for retail behavioural PD models (red below 0.50), and the relative decrease from development to out-of-time is 2.8%, well below the 10% amber threshold. The small difference between development and out-of-sample performance and the limited decrease out-of-time indicate that the model is not overfitted, and PD-MORT-NL v3 applied to the same out-of-time sample reaches a Gini of 0.742. The ROC curves and Gini coefficients per calendar year are shown in Annex 7. The PSI of the score distribution between the development sample and the out-of-time sample is 0.07 for S1 and 0.05 for S2, and the PSI of every risk driver is below 0.10. The Gini coefficient per calendar year ranges from 0.78 to 0.83 without trend, and the coefficients re-estimated on 2012–2016 and on 2017–2022 lie within the 95% confidence intervals of the development coefficients for all drivers. The 12-month migration matrix on 2023–2024 shows 81.2% of obligors in the same grade and 1.9% migrating by more than two grades, consistent with the hybrid rating philosophy.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses covered the key assumptions, parameters and input data: including the excluded facilities changes the long-run average by +0.01 percentage points; a calibration window of 2016–2024 instead of 2012–2024 lowers it from 0.44% to 0.30%; a default definition based on days past due only lowers it by 0.06 percentage points; and a regression imputation of debt-to-income raises the average PD by 0.3%. The material expert judgements were tested under reasonable alternatives: a single-segment model (EJ-PDM4-02) lowers the Gini to 0.771, removing the forced NHG flag (EJ-PDM4-04) changes the grade of 0.9% of exposures, and LTV caps of 200% and 300% (EJ-PDM4-03) have no effect on the grade distribution. The results feed the quantification of the MoC in chapter 6, notably the calibration-window sensitivity, which shows the importance of retaining the downturn years 2012–2014 in the long-run average.

sections.heading: Fair treatment testing and analysis of individual defaults
sections.text: Before approval the final model was tested for disparate outcomes across groups defined by gender and age band, using the metrics and thresholds of AI-STD-700: the ratio of average grade PDs between groups ranges from 0.93 to 1.08 and the difference in the share of obligors in grades R07–R12 is below 1.2 percentage points, within the thresholds. After controlling for arrears history the remaining differences are not significant, and the outcome testing is repeated annually in the model review. The results of the proxy screening (RDS §7.4) and of this outcome testing are documented in the RDS documentation and in this MDD. A sample of 150 defaults from grades R01–R04 in 2021–2024 was reviewed file by file to verify that the main drivers of default are reflected in the model: 61% followed a sudden income loss (unemployment, illness or divorce), 22% a business failure of self-employed obligors and 17% other causes, and in 79% of cases the obligor had migrated to a worse grade in the months before default. Self-employed income type was added as a driver partly because of this analysis; no model adjustment was made for singular events such as fraud cases.

sections.heading: Material assumptions and circumstances where the model does not work effectively
sections.text: The material assumptions are: the approximated default flag for 2012–2015 represents defaults under the current definition up to the MoC; the effects of the drivers are stable over time; indexed collateral values reflect market values; and the portfolio remains within the range of application; each assumption was assessed for plausibility and is tested in chapter 7 or monitored. The model does not work effectively for loans without a collateral valuation, for interest-only loans at or after contractual maturity, for newly introduced mortgage products with features not observed in the RDS, and in the event of a house-price decline beyond the 2012–2013 experience; such cases are identified in monitoring and escalated for an assessment of an overlay.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan
sections.text: The monitoring plan of PD-MORT-NL v4 forms this chapter; it will be approved by the model owner before go-live and has been shared with Model Validation for review. It defines for each KPI the calculation, the amber and red thresholds, the quarterly frequency, the data and reference periods, the segments and grades at which it is computed, the responsible persons (monitoring analyst of Retail Credit Risk Modelling, reviewed by the model owner) and the escalation and actions per traffic light. The KPIs cover discriminatory power, calibration per grade and portfolio, score and driver stability, rating migration, production data quality, overrides, overlays and model coverage, and are computed for the whole model, per segment and per grade. The plan is updated at every model change and reviewed at least annually, and quarterly results are reported within 60 calendar days after the end of the reference quarter.

sections.heading: Escalation and annual review
sections.text: A red result on any KPI triggers a review by the model owner and notification of Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days; red results are reported to the Model Risk Committee. Realised default rates are compared with the grade PDs quarterly and in the annual review; where realised default rates continue to exceed the expected range, taking the economic cycle into account, the estimates are revised upward through recalibration or an overlay. A red monitoring outcome or an annual review concluding that the estimates are inadequate leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the Model Risk Committee within three months, and monitoring results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and for an additional MoC. Back-testing uses the longest available history from 2012 and the methods and data are documented in the monitoring plan and updated at least annually; changes in validation methods or data are documented.

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: Expert judgement applied in the development is recorded in the expert judgement log EJL-MDL01-v4, stored with this MDD, and described here with reference to the log entries: EJ-PDM4-01 mapping of historical product codes (data treatment, low); EJ-PDM4-02 segmentation by arrears in the last 12 months (design, medium); EJ-PDM4-03 capping of indexed LTV at 250% (data treatment, low); EJ-PDM4-04 forced inclusion of the NHG flag (design, low); EJ-PDM4-05 retention of the non-monotone binning of loan age (design, low); EJ-PDM4-06 quantification of MoC B2 (MoC, medium). Each entry records the type, life-cycle stage and affected data, segment or parameter, the rationale with the evidence relied on and the alternatives rejected, the quantified impact, the proposer, the approver and the date of approval, and a review date with expiry conditions. The rationales are specific: for example, EJ-PDM4-02 cites the Gini difference of 0.018 and the weight-of-evidence patterns per segment, so a knowledgeable third party can replicate its effect.

sections.heading: Materiality, approval and challenge of expert judgement
sections.text: Each judgement is classified by its impact on the average PD and on grade assignments against the best statistical alternative: EJ-PDM4-02 and EJ-PDM4-06 are medium, the others low; the aggregate effect of all judgements is +1.9% on the average PD and a grade change for 2.6% of exposures, below the high materiality threshold of MRM-STD-023 §4.2. Low-materiality judgements were approved by the model owner and medium-materiality judgements by the model owner and the head of the modelling unit, never by their proposer alone, and all medium judgements were challenged beforehand by a Retail Credit Risk Management expert independent of the proposer, with the challenge and resolution recorded in the log. No judgement has an unquantifiable impact, and each is reviewed at the annual model review and when new data could replace it. How expert judgement and model results are combined, and the monitoring of their impact, is described in this chapter and in chapter 10.

sections.heading: Override policy
sections.text: Overrides of the grade are permitted only within the override policy for retail mortgages: the closed list of reasons comprises OR-01 confirmed fraud, OR-02 known loss of income not yet visible in the data, OR-03 divorce or death of a co-borrower, OR-04 pending forced sale and OR-05 other information from a credit review; only downgrades of at most three grades are permitted, and upgrades are not permitted. Each override records the reason code, a written rationale, the supporting evidence, the proposer from Retail Collections and the approver from Retail Credit Risk Management, who is independent of the proposer. Override rates, direction and magnitude are monitored quarterly per reason and approving unit, and the performance of overridden obligors is compared annually with non-overridden obligors by original and final grade (see chapter 10).

sections.heading: Purpose and regulatory use
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL v4 estimates the 12-month probability of default of Dutch residential mortgage obligors for the calculation of own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach (CRR Articles 143 and 180) and replaces PD-MORT-NL v3, approved by the ECB in 2022. The model assigns every obligor in the range of application to one of the 12 non-defaulted grades of the retail master scale, and the grade PD is used in the own funds calculation, in credit risk appetite metrics (expected loss, RWA density and grade distribution of the mortgage book), in risk-adjusted pricing of the mortgage offer, in internal capital allocation to Retail Banking and in management reporting. The secondary use is the prioritisation of arrears management: Retail Collections uses the monthly grade to set contact intensity for obligors in S2, and the early-warning monitoring of CR-POL-001 §10.1 uses a downgrade of three or more grades as an early-warning indicator for review within 30 days. Credit decisions on new mortgages and on restructuring or renewal of existing mortgages require a valid grade from the approved rating system: new applications are graded with the application variant of the scorecard at origination, and existing obligors receive their monthly behavioural grade from PD-MORT-NL. The model is used only within the range of application in §1.2.

sections.heading: Range of application
sections.text: The range of application comprises all owner-occupied residential mortgage loans to natural persons in the Netherlands in the retail exposure class secured by immovable property, including the migrated former brand portfolio; at 31 December 2026 it contained 376,900 facilities of 164,300 obligors with an EAD of EUR 37.4 billion and RWEA of EUR 4,436 million under v3. Buy-to-let mortgages, mortgages to legal entities and commercial real estate are outside the range of application and are rated by other rating systems; the assignment to the retail exposure class and to this rating system follows the exposure class methodology and is performed automatically in the credit risk engine. The IRB approach is applied to all exposures of the retail mortgage exposure type, and no exposures in the range of application are under permanent partial use of the Standardised Approach. Extensions of the range of application to new products or obligor types are assessed under MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 before use, including the demonstration of representativeness and comparability.

sections.heading: Users and parameters used for internal purposes
sections.text: The main users are Credit Risk Reporting (own funds calculation), Retail Credit Risk Management (risk appetite and portfolio steering), Retail Collections (arrears management), Finance (capital allocation) and Mortgage Pricing. The IFRS 9 ECL model for residential mortgages (MDL-07) does not use the IRB PD directly but uses the PD-MORT-NL v4 grade as an input; where IRB PDs are used for purposes that require unbiased estimates, the MoC and the regulatory floor are removed and the removal is documented in the user guide. Pricing uses the grade PD including MoC, identical to the own funds parameter, so no difference arises between internal and regulatory parameters for that use. The known limitations of chapter 8 and the conditions attached to the approval are communicated to users in the PD-MORT-NL v4 user guide and in the credit risk manual for Retail Collections. The grade is not used for any decision based solely on automated processing: arrears management actions are taken by collection officers who see the main drivers of the grade and may deviate from the suggested contact strategy, so Art. 22 GDPR does not apply to the use of the model.

sections.heading: Tier, materiality and complexity
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL is a Tier 1 model: materiality is High on exposure and own funds impact (the largest retail IRB portfolio of the Bank) and complexity is Medium (statistical model with two segments, approximated historical default data and several expert judgements), which leads to Tier 1 in the materiality-by-complexity matrix of MRM-STD-010 §6.4. The tier was proposed by the model owner with the tiering template, approved by Model Risk Management on 22 September 2026 and will be confirmed at the initial validation; it exceeds the minimum Tier 2 for models used for own funds requirements. The tier is reviewed at least annually and at every material change; the last review on 15 March 2027 confirmed Tier 1. The complexity assessment under the ECB guide classifies the model as not highly complex (no machine-learning technique, no dynamic recalibration), and the rating system is classified as material in the Bank's IRB materiality assessment communicated to the ECB in the annual IRB roll-out and materiality report. As a Tier 1 IRB model, PD-MORT-NL v4 is validated before first use, annually thereafter and in full scope at least every three years.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The rating system consists of six separated components in line with CRM-STD-100 §4.3: (a) two segment-specific logistic regression scorecards (risk differentiation); (b) the assignment of scores to the 12 grades of the retail master scale; (c) the calibration of grade PDs to the long-run average default rate per calibration segment; (d) the margin of conservatism; (e) the regulatory PD floor; and (f) the override process. The risk differentiation step (chapter 4) and the risk quantification step (chapters 5 and 6) are developed, documented and tested separately, and both meet CRR Art. 179 and CRM-STD-100. Obligors are assigned to grades on the basis of obligor characteristics (income type, debt-service-to-income at origination, arrears and payment behaviour), transaction characteristics (interest-only share, loan age, NHG guarantee, indexed loan-to-value of the collateral) and delinquency (days past due, arrears history and forbearance). PD is assigned at obligor level: property-related drivers are computed over all loan parts secured by the same property, arrears drivers over all facilities of the obligor, and all facilities of an obligor receive the same grade.

sections.heading: Segmentation and rating philosophy
sections.text: The population is split into two segments that are also the calibration segments: S1 comprises obligors without any day past due above the materiality threshold in the previous 12 months (98.6% of observations, long-run average default rate 0.29%), and S2 obligors with at least one such day in the previous 12 months (1.4% of observations, long-run average default rate 11.2%). The segmentation is an expert judgement in model design (EJ-PDM4-02), supported by the finding that arrears variables dominate the risk ranking in S2 while they carry no information in S1, and by a single-model alternative that has an out-of-time Gini of 0.771 against 0.789 for the segmented model. Separate scorecards per segment lead to grades with homogeneous risk: within S1 the ranking is driven by collateral and affordability, within S2 by the severity and recency of arrears. PD-MORT-NL v4 follows the Bank's hybrid rating philosophy of CRM-STD-100 §4.2: grade assignment responds to current conditions through indexed LTV (house prices) and payment behaviour, while the PD per grade is calibrated to the long-run average default rate. In a downturn obligors are expected to migrate to worse grades while grade-level default rates remain broadly stable; over 2012–2024 the share of obligors in grades R07–R12 fell from 6.9% (2013) to 3.1% (2024), while the yearly default rate of each grade stayed within ±30% of its long-run average, which is consistent with the chosen philosophy. The rating philosophy, including the assumptions on net migration across grades, is unchanged from PD-MORT-NL v3.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and processes
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL v4 uses the output of the collateral indexation process (regional CBS/Kadaster index) and of the automated valuation model for the indexed LTV, and it provides grades and PDs to LGD-MORT-NL (expected loss best estimate), to the IFRS 9 mortgage model (MDL-07) and to the ICAAP credit risk stress test. In the ICAAP and EBA stress tests the grade distribution is projected under the severe but plausible recession scenarios of the Bank by shocking house prices and unemployment, and the resulting rating migration and effect on own funds requirements are reported to the Asset and Liability Committee; in the 2026 ICAAP adverse scenario the average PD of the portfolio increased by a factor of 2.4. The stress-test projection uses a satellite model that approximates grade migration from house-price and unemployment shocks; this approximation, its back-test on 2012–2014 and its limitations are documented in the stress-test methodology and referenced in the stress-test reports.

sections.heading: Changes relative to PD-MORT-NL v3
sections.text: PD-MORT-NL v4 changes the rating system as follows: the observation period is extended from 2012–2019 to 2012–2024; the single scorecard of v3 is replaced by two segment scorecards; five risk drivers are new (interest-only share, loan age, self-employed income type, payment reminders and months since last cure) and three v3 drivers are removed (original LTV, borrower age band and product type); and the MoC is re-quantified under CRM-STD-101 v2.0. Rank ordering changes significantly: the Spearman rank correlation between v3 and v4 scores on the December 2026 portfolio is 0.86, below the significance level of 0.90 defined in the Bank's change policy, and 34.6% of exposures change grade. The master scale, the definition of default, the override policy and the rating philosophy are unchanged. The classification of the change is documented in the model change memorandum CHG-2026-0417.

sections.heading: Reference data set
sections.text: Development and calibration use the frozen RDS RDS-MORT-NL-v4.0, documented in the approved RDS documentation (Dataset Construction and DQ Assessment – Residential Real Estate Mortgages, version 1.0): 9,600,412 account-months of 780,000 facilities from monthly snapshots January 2012 to December 2024, with 43,118 observations followed by a default within 12 months. The RDS draws on internal data only: the mortgage administration system, the arrears management system and the collateral valuation database, complemented by the regional house-price index for collateral indexation. All relevant and current information available for the portfolio is used in the grade assignment: the monthly snapshot of contract, collateral and arrears data is complete for 99.4% of the critical data elements, and debt-to-income at origination is imputed conservatively where missing.

sections.heading: Development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples
sections.text: The samples were defined in the development plan before estimation: observations from January 2012 to December 2022 were split at obligor level into a development sample (70%: 5,684,210 observations, 27,075 defaults) and an out-of-sample holdout (30%: 2,436,090 observations, 11,603 defaults), and all observations from January 2023 to December 2024 form the out-of-time sample (1,480,112 observations, 4,440 defaults). The out-of-time sample was not used for variable selection or parameter estimation; it was used only for performance testing and for the calibration tests in §5.4. Observations are weighted by the inverse of the number of facilities of the obligor in the snapshot, so that obligors with several loan parts are not overweighted. Default rates are 0.48% in the development and out-of-sample data and 0.30% in the out-of-time sample, reflecting the benign conditions of 2023–2024.

sections.heading: Definition of default and data deficiencies
sections.text: The target is the default of the obligor under CR-STD-110 within 12 months after the snapshot; the definitions of default and the historical approximations are documented in RDS §3.2–3.8, and their consistency with CRR Art. 178 is demonstrated in the Definition of Default implementation memo. The same default events are used for PD-MORT-NL v4 and LGD-MORT-NL. Because the RDS combines three default-definition regimes (approximated 2012–2015, re-derived 2016–2020 and register-based from 2021), their effect on the estimates is reflected by segment-specific tests and by the category A MoC in chapter 6. Risk differentiation under the current definition is demonstrated on the time series 2021–2024 of realised default rates per grade, which is based entirely on the default register under CR-STD-110 v2.0: the out-of-time Gini on 2023–2024 is 0.789 and the Gini on the 2021–2022 out-of-sample observations is 0.796. The five data deficiencies of RDS §6.7 are treated as follows: DD-01 (approximated default flag 2012–2015) is covered by MoC A1; DD-02 (imputed debt-to-income at origination) by MoC A2; DD-03 and DD-05 (exclusions) by the appropriate adjustment AA-01 and MoC A3; DD-04 (missing valuation method before 2019) has no effect on the model variables and requires no treatment. Each deficiency is recorded in the limitations log (LIM-01 to LIM-04) and in the MoC register with a reference to the data deficiency log entry. The expert judgement applied in the treatment of DD-02 (imputation with the segment median, EJ-PDM4-03 for the related LTV capping) is linked to the assessment of MoC A2 in §6.2.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives
sections.text: Four alternatives were assessed against the criteria of MRM-STD-020 §6.1 (regulatory requirements, data, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation): (1) segmented logistic regression scorecards; (2) a gradient boosting model (LightGBM); (3) a discrete-time hazard model; and (4) the v3 single scorecard re-estimated on the new RDS. Out-of-time Gini coefficients were 0.789, 0.801, 0.781 and 0.763 respectively; the gradient boosting model performs slightly better but is less transparent, less stable over time (PSI of the score 0.12 against 0.07) and would require the explainability controls of AI-STD-700, while the hazard model offers no gain for a 12-month horizon. The segmented logistic regression is selected because it is conceptually sound for a 12-month default horizon, consistent with the pool-based treatment of retail exposures, fully interpretable at driver level and implementable in the existing rating engine; the performance difference with the gradient boosting model (0.012 Gini) is not considered material. The logistic regression models the log-odds of default within 12 months as a linear function of weight-of-evidence transformed risk drivers, estimated by weighted maximum likelihood; its assumptions (independence of observations conditional on the drivers, linearity in the weight-of-evidence scale, stability of driver effects over time) are tested in §4.4 and chapter 7.

sections.heading: Long list of candidate risk drivers
sections.text: The long list of 38 candidate drivers combines the drivers of v3, variables proposed in two expert workshops with Retail Credit Risk Management and Retail Collections (28 October and 4 November 2026) and new data available since 2019; it covers collateral, affordability, product, payment behaviour, arrears history and forbearance. For each candidate the expected direction of the effect on PD was recorded before estimation (for example positive for indexed LTV, interest-only share and payment reminders, negative for months since last cure), together with its economic rationale, availability at the point of use in the monthly production run and stability over the observation period. Climate-related and environmental risk drivers were assessed: the energy label of the property (available for 81% of facilities) and a flood-risk indicator for the location showed no significant additional explanatory power after controlling for indexed LTV (p-values 0.21 and 0.47), so they are not included; their materiality is reassessed in each annual review. Credit bureau data (BKR) are used only at origination and are not model inputs, so no adjustment for outdated bureau or financial statement information is needed. Borrower age, gender and nationality were not offered as candidates, in line with CR-POL-001 §9 and the proxy screening of RDS §7.4.

sections.heading: Univariate analysis and seasoning
sections.text: Each candidate was binned (at most eight bins, minimum 5% of observations per bin, monotone weight of evidence unless economically justified) and assessed on the development sample for information value, univariate Gini, the stability of its weight of evidence across the calendar years 2012–2022 and the share of missing values. Candidates with an information value below 0.02, with a sign of the weight of evidence contradicting the expected direction, or with a PSI above 0.10 between 2012–2016 and 2017–2022 were removed; 24 of the 38 candidates passed this step. The non-monotone relation of loan age with default risk (a peak between 24 and 60 months after origination) was kept because it reflects the seasoning pattern described below. Seasoning was analysed by origination cohort: 12-month default rates rise during the first two years after origination, peak between 24 and 60 months and decline thereafter, and this pattern is stable across the cohorts 2012–2020. Loan age is included as a risk driver in S1, so the expected change of the PD over the life of the exposure is reflected in the grade assignment; in S2 loan age has no additional explanatory power once arrears are known. Interest-only loans originated before 2013 reach contractual maturity from 2030 onwards; because the RDS contains no maturities of such loans, the refinancing risk at maturity is recorded as limitation LIM-05.

sections.heading: Multivariate selection and final model
sections.text: Among pairs of candidates with a Spearman correlation above 0.6 the candidate with the higher information value was kept, and stepwise selection per segment (entry at p < 0.01, retention at p < 0.001) was followed by an expert review of the selected set, which forced the NHG flag into S1 (EJ-PDM4-04); the variance inflation factors of the final drivers are below 1.9. The final S1 scorecard contains seven drivers (indexed LTV, interest-only share, loan age, NHG guarantee, debt-service-to-income at origination, self-employed income type and number of payment reminders in the last 24 months), and the final S2 scorecard contains six drivers (current days-past-due bucket, maximum days past due in the last 12 months, months since last cure, indexed LTV, arrears amount relative to the monthly instalment and forbearance in the last 24 months). All coefficients on the weight-of-evidence scale are positive and significant at 0.1%, which confirms the expected direction of every driver, and their magnitudes are plausible (for example, an increase of indexed LTV from 60–80% to above 100% raises the odds of default in S1 by a factor of 2.7). The drivers form a reasonable and effective basis for the prediction, cover the material drivers identified in the expert workshops, show no material bias across regions, product types or origination cohorts, and do not distort own funds requirements.

sections.heading: Final scorecards and replication
sections.text: The scorecard points are scaled to 600 points at odds of 50:1 with 20 points to double the odds, and the full specification (bins, weights of evidence, coefficients, points per bin and score cut-offs per grade) is given in Annex 4 and in parameter file pd_mort_nl_v4_params.json of tag v4.0.3. The grade assignment is fully determined by the scorecards and the cut-offs, so Model Validation and other third parties can replicate the assignment of every observation from the RDS and the parameter file, and the rating criteria are applied identically for all distribution channels, regions and business units. All drivers are measured at the monthly snapshot date and relate to the same 12-month horizon in development, calibration and application. Production computes the score monthly from the same fields and transformations, as specified in the implementation specification.

sections.heading: Treatment of missing values and outliers in estimation
sections.text: Missing values are classified per variable: debt-to-income at origination is missing because of a data deficiency (2.3%, DD-02) and is imputed with the segment median of the origination year; months since last cure is structurally missing for obligors that never had arrears and is assigned its own bin; no other driver has missing values above 0.1%. The imputation is performed by the build code and is reproducible; re-estimating the S1 scorecard with a regression imputation instead of the segment median changes the average PD by +0.3% and the Gini by less than 0.001, and the residual uncertainty is covered by MoC A2. Indexed LTV is capped at 250% (EJ-PDM4-03), which affects 0.02% of observations, all in the highest LTV bin; the cap is applied identically in development and production, and caps at 200% or 300% leave the Gini and the grade distribution unchanged.

sections.heading: Calibration target, long-run average and calibration sample
sections.text: Grade PDs are calibrated per calibration segment to the long-run average of one-year default rates, defined as the arithmetic average of the one-year default rates at the 52 quarter-end reference dates from March 2012 to December 2024 computed with overlapping one-year windows as described in RDS §2.5. The long-run average default rate is 0.44% for the portfolio, 0.29% for S1 and 11.2% for S2, after the appropriate adjustment AA-01 for the exclusions (+0.01 percentage points on the portfolio level). Overlapping quarterly windows were chosen after analysing the alternatives: the long-run average based on non-overlapping January windows differs by 0.006 percentage points, seasonality of defaults within the year is not significant, and short-term contracts do not occur in the portfolio. The calibration is consistent with the definition of default used for the target variable. The calibration sample of each calibration segment consists of all obligors in the range of application at the 52 quarter-end reference dates from March 2012 to December 2024 (8.37 million obligor-dates, of which 116,200 in S2), scored with the final scorecards. The calibration sample is stored read-only as RDS-MORT-NL-v4.0-CAL next to the frozen RDS, and its construction is part of tag v4.0.0 of the build code. Obligors that change segment between reference dates are included in the segment in which they are at the reference date.

sections.heading: Representativeness of the long-run average period
sections.text: The observation period includes the most recent five years and all earlier years with facility-level data, and it contains the 2012–2014 downturn with the highest default rates of the available history. The period is therefore considered to reflect the likely range of variability of default rates, and no upward adjustment of the long-run average is applied; no adjustment lowers the long-run average below the observed average. Facility-level data before 2012 are not available, so the long-run average cannot be compared with the reference period 2008–2018; the aggregate annual 90-days arrears rates of the predecessor system for 2009–2011 (0.52% to 0.71%) are below the 2012–2013 default rates, which indicates that the observation period is not less severe than the years preceding it. The long-run average of v4 (0.44%) is lower than that of v3 (0.54% over 2012–2019) because the extended window adds the five benign years 2020–2024, which shows that the estimates reflect the new data that have become available since the last development.

sections.heading: Calibration method, grade assignment and PD floor
sections.text: Calibration is performed per calibration segment by shifting the intercept of the scorecard so that the average calibrated PD over the calibration sample equals the segment long-run average; the shift preserves the rank ordering of obligors within the segment. Each obligor is then assigned to the grade of the retail master scale (R01–R12, with RD for defaulted obligors) whose PD boundaries of CRM-STD-100 §5.2 contain its calibrated PD, and the grade PD is the average calibrated PD of the grade in the calibration sample; continuous PDs are not used in the own funds calculation. Grade PDs before MoC are R01 0.06%, R02 0.14%, R03 0.27%, R04 0.46%, R05 0.78%, R06 1.33%, R07 2.28%, R08 4.05%, R09 7.30%, R10 13.9%, R11 25.8% and R12 47.5%; each grade maps to exactly one master scale grade and PDs increase monotonically with grade. Calibration is performed after overrides are taken into account (overridden obligors enter with their final grade) and before the application of the MoC and the regulatory PD floor. Grade assignments are refreshed monthly in production and therefore at least annually for every obligor. The PD applied to each exposure is floored at 0.05% in accordance with CRR Art. 163(1) and CRM-STD-100 §11.1, after the MoC; the lowest final grade PD is 0.07% (R01), so the floor is not binding for any grade. The floor is applied at exposure level in the production engine, and the share of exposures and EAD for which it is binding (0% at 31 December 2026) is reported in the quarterly monitoring report.

sections.heading: Calibration tests
sections.text: For each of the 52 reference dates the average best-estimate PD per calibration segment was compared with the one-year default rate and with the long-run average default rate: in S1 the average PD ranges from 0.25% to 0.36% against one-year default rates of 0.12% to 0.58%, and in S2 from 10.1% to 12.6% against 7.9% to 15.8%, a pattern consistent with a hybrid rating philosophy. Per grade, the Jeffreys test of the best-estimate PD against the default rate over the full calibration sample shows no grade with p < 5%, and the long-run default rate of every grade lies within ±12% of its grade PD. Qualitative calibration analyses confirm a unimodal distribution of obligors over the grades, a minimum of 1,100 obligors per grade at every reference date after 2014 and no excessive concentration (§5.5). Calibration test results on the out-of-time sample are reported in §7.2.

sections.heading: Grade distribution, homogeneity and concentration
sections.text: At 31 December 2026 the largest grade, R02, contains 28.4% of the exposures of the rating system, below the 30% limit of CRM-STD-100 §5.4, and the number-weighted Herfindahl index of the grade distribution is 0.19. Homogeneity within grades was tested by comparing the default rate of subsets defined by NHG, interest-only share, origination cohort, region and self-employed status with the rest of the grade (chi-square test at 5%); 3 of 96 tests are significant, which is within the number expected by chance, and no material subset shows a significantly different default rate. Heterogeneity between adjacent grades was tested with one-sided z-tests on the long-run default rates: all adjacent pairs differ significantly at 1% except R11 and R12 (p = 0.032), which are kept separate because of the large difference in PD (25.8% against 47.5%) and the small number of obligors in R12. The number of exposures in each grade is sufficient for meaningful quantification and validation, with at least 1,100 obligors and 60 default events per grade over the observation period.

sections.heading: Identification of deficiencies and appropriate adjustments
sections.text: Deficiencies were identified systematically with the trigger list of Annex 1 of CRM-STD-101, covering RDS completeness, the definition of default, methods, systems and processes, underwriting and policies, the environment and the estimation error. Five deficiencies were identified, and each was assigned to exactly one category and recorded in the MoC register: category A – A1 approximated default flag 2012–2015, A2 imputation of debt-to-income at origination, A3 exclusions; category B – B1 changes in underwriting standards 2013–2018, B2 payment deferrals and support measures in 2020–2021; the general estimation error is covered by category C per segment. Three triggers were considered and rejected: the migration of the collateral database in 2019 (no effect on model variables), the centralisation of collections in 2016 (captured by the arrears drivers, no break in default rates) and the low number of defaults (not applicable, all segments have more than 14,000 default observations). The deficiencies raised in the validation of v3 (V3-F01 on the calibration of the arrears segment and V3-F02 on self-employed obligors) were assessed and are addressed by the segmentation and by the self-employed risk driver, so no MoC component was added for them. For each deficiency an appropriate adjustment was considered first: for A3 the long-run average is increased by 0.01 percentage points (adjustment AA-01), which neutralises the effect of the exclusions quantified in RDS §4.2, and the remaining uncertainty of the adjustment is covered by MoC A3. For A1 no appropriate adjustment is applied because the undercount of default events in 2012–2015 cannot be estimated reliably year by year; the effect is covered in full by MoC A1. For B1 and B2 no adjustment is possible because the counterfactual default rates are not observable; the adjusted long-run average of 0.44% is the best estimate of the portfolio default rate over the cycle.

sections.heading: Category A MoC
sections.text: MoC A1 (+6.0%) covers the approximated default flag for 2012–2015: applying the approximation rule of RDS §3.2 to the 2016 data, for which the CR-STD-110 components are available, yields 5.7% fewer default events than the flag under the current definition, and the MoC is set at +6% relative on the long-run average of both segments. MoC A2 (+0.5%) covers the imputation of debt-to-income at origination, based on the sensitivity to the alternative imputation method in §4.6 (+0.3%) rounded up. MoC A3 (+0.5%) covers the uncertainty of adjustment AA-01, based on the range of default rates of the excluded facilities (0.41% to 0.53% at a 90% confidence level). Category A MoC is quantified per calibration segment and totals +7.0% in S1 and S2; it covers both the uncertainty from the appropriate adjustment and the uncorrected deficiencies, and each component is non-negative.

sections.heading: Category B and category C MoC
sections.text: MoC B1 (+2.0% in both segments) covers the changes in underwriting standards between 2013 and 2018 (reduction of the LTV limit and the amortisation requirement), which lower the default risk of recent cohorts in a way that the long-run average of older cohorts does not reflect fully; it is quantified by comparing the long-run average with and without the cohorts originated before 2013. MoC B2 (+1.5% in S1, +1.0% in S2) covers the payment deferrals and government support of 2020–2021, which may have suppressed default rates in those years; it is based on expert judgement (EJ-PDM4-06) because neither re-estimation nor benchmarking can reproduce the counterfactual default rates, and it was approved by the model owner and the head of the modelling unit. Category B MoC totals +3.5% in S1 and +3.0% in S2. MoC C covers the general estimation error of the long-run average: for each segment the one-sided 90% upper confidence bound of the long-run average was derived from a block bootstrap of the quarterly one-year default rates (block length four quarters, 5,000 replications), which accounts for the autocorrelation of default rates. MoC C is +9.0% in S1 and +6.1% in S2; it is larger in S1 because of the higher relative volatility of its yearly default rates and is greater than zero in both segments. Grade-level MoC is not used; the MoC reflects estimation uncertainty at the level of the final grade PDs because the segment add-on is applied proportionally to every grade of the segment.

sections.heading: Aggregation and application of the MoC
sections.text: The total MoC per calibration segment is the simple sum of the category A, B and C components without diversification: +19.5% in S1 and +16.1% in S2, equivalent to +18.3% on the portfolio long-run average. So that each grade has a single final PD, the MoC of a grade is the average of the segment MoCs weighted by the share of each segment in that grade in the calibration sample: +19.5% for R01–R06, decreasing to +16.1% for R12. The final PD of each grade is its best estimate plus the MoC and is then subject to the regulatory floor: final grade PDs are R01 0.07%, R02 0.17%, R03 0.32%, R04 0.55%, R05 0.93%, R06 1.59%, R07 2.71%, R08 4.80%, R09 8.58%, R10 16.3%, R11 30.1% and R12 55.1%. Because the grade add-ons decrease only gradually from 19.5% to 16.1% while best-estimate PDs increase by at least 70% from one grade to the next, the MoC preserves the rank ordering and final PDs increase monotonically with grade and remain within the boundaries of their master scale grade. The total MoC is below 20% of the best estimate, so the redevelopment trigger of CRM-STD-101 §7.2 is not met, and the MoC is quantified in accordance with paragraphs 36–52 of EBA/GL/2017/16.

sections.heading: MoC register, reporting and remediation
sections.text: The MoC register of PD-MORT-NL v4 records for each deficiency the category, the affected components and calibration segments, the quantification method, the MoC value, the related data deficiency log entry and the remediation status, and this chapter together with the register constitutes the list of all identified deficiencies required in the model documentation. Every category A deficiency has a remediation plan with owner and target date or is documented as permanent: A1 and A3 are permanent (historical data no longer exist) and are reassessed at each annual review, and A2 is remediated at source by 31 December 2027. MoC levels are monitored in the annual review of estimates and reported internally separately for categories A, B and C; the effect of the MoC on RWEA at 31 December 2026 is EUR 212 million (A EUR 81 million, B EUR 41 million, C EUR 90 million). An MoC component is reduced or removed only after the underlying deficiency has been remediated and Model Validation has confirmed the remediation, and any change of the MoC is processed as a model change under MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power and stability
sections.text: Discriminatory power was measured on the development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples for the whole model and per segment: the Gini coefficient is 0.812, 0.806 and 0.789 for the whole model (out-of-time 95% DeLong interval 0.776–0.802), 0.662, 0.655 and 0.641 for S1, and 0.583, 0.577 and 0.561 for S2. All values are above the thresholds of MV-HB-003 for retail behavioural PD models (red below 0.50), and the relative decrease from development to out-of-time is 2.8%, well below the 10% amber threshold. The small difference between development and out-of-sample performance and the limited decrease out-of-time indicate that the model is not overfitted, and PD-MORT-NL v3 applied to the same out-of-time sample reaches a Gini of 0.742. The ROC curves and Gini coefficients per calendar year are shown in Annex 7. The PSI of the score distribution between the development sample and the out-of-time sample is 0.07 for S1 and 0.05 for S2, and the PSI of every risk driver is below 0.10. The Gini coefficient per calendar year ranges from 0.78 to 0.83 without trend, and the coefficients re-estimated on 2012–2016 and on 2017–2022 lie within the 95% confidence intervals of the development coefficients for all drivers. The 12-month migration matrix on 2023–2024 shows 81.2% of obligors in the same grade and 1.9% migrating by more than two grades, consistent with the hybrid rating philosophy.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and margin of conservatism
sections.text: The approximation of the default flag for 2012–2015 is treated as a category A data deficiency. A MoC of +6% relative is applied to the long-run average default rate. The full MoC, including categories B and C, is set out in chapter 6. On the out-of-time sample (2023–2024) the average best-estimate PD is 0.36% against an observed default rate of 0.30%, and the Jeffreys test does not indicate underestimation at portfolio level (p = 0.99). Per grade, 11 of the 12 grades have a Jeffreys p-value of at least 5%; grade R09 has p = 0.031 (amber), which concerns 1 of 12 grades and is analysed in the limitations log (LIM-07). After MoC no grade shows a p-value below 5%.

sections.heading: Challenger model and benchmarks
sections.text: As required for Tier 1 models, PD-MORT-NL v4 was compared with a challenger model (gradient boosting with the same 38 candidates) and with PD-MORT-NL v3: the challenger reaches an out-of-time Gini of 0.801 and v3 0.742 against 0.789 for v4. The challenger outperforms v4 by 0.012 Gini, which is within the confidence interval and is not considered material; its gains come mainly from interactions between arrears variables in S2, and the choice of the scorecard is justified by interpretability, stability and implementation in §4.1. As an external comparison, the average final PD of the portfolio (0.53%) lies within the range of Dutch residential mortgage PDs published in the Pillar 3 reports of four peer banks for 2025 (0.38% to 0.94%), and default rates in the RDS follow the same pattern over time as the national 90-days arrears statistics of the BKR credit register.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses covered the key assumptions, parameters and input data: including the excluded facilities changes the long-run average by +0.01 percentage points; a calibration window of 2016–2024 instead of 2012–2024 lowers it from 0.44% to 0.30%; a default definition based on days past due only lowers it by 0.06 percentage points; and a regression imputation of debt-to-income raises the average PD by 0.3%. The material expert judgements were tested under reasonable alternatives: a single-segment model (EJ-PDM4-02) lowers the Gini to 0.771, removing the forced NHG flag (EJ-PDM4-04) changes the grade of 0.9% of exposures, and LTV caps of 200% and 300% (EJ-PDM4-03) have no effect on the grade distribution. The results feed the quantification of the MoC in chapter 6, notably the calibration-window sensitivity, which shows the importance of retaining the downturn years 2012–2014 in the long-run average.

sections.heading: Fair treatment testing and analysis of individual defaults
sections.text: Before approval the final model was tested for disparate outcomes across groups defined by gender and age band, using the metrics and thresholds of AI-STD-700: the ratio of average grade PDs between groups ranges from 0.93 to 1.08 and the difference in the share of obligors in grades R07–R12 is below 1.2 percentage points, within the thresholds. After controlling for arrears history the remaining differences are not significant, and the outcome testing is repeated annually in the model review. The results of the proxy screening (RDS §7.4) and of this outcome testing are documented in the RDS documentation and in this MDD. A sample of 150 defaults from grades R01–R04 in 2021–2024 was reviewed file by file to verify that the main drivers of default are reflected in the model: 61% followed a sudden income loss (unemployment, illness or divorce), 22% a business failure of self-employed obligors and 17% other causes, and in 79% of cases the obligor had migrated to a worse grade in the months before default. Self-employed income type was added as a driver partly because of this analysis; no model adjustment was made for singular events such as fraud cases.

sections.heading: Material assumptions and circumstances where the model does not work effectively
sections.text: The material assumptions are: the approximated default flag for 2012–2015 represents defaults under the current definition up to the MoC; the effects of the drivers are stable over time; indexed collateral values reflect market values; and the portfolio remains within the range of application; each assumption was assessed for plausibility and is tested in chapter 7 or monitored. The model does not work effectively for loans without a collateral valuation, for interest-only loans at or after contractual maturity, for newly introduced mortgage products with features not observed in the RDS, and in the event of a house-price decline beyond the 2012–2013 experience; such cases are identified in monitoring and escalated for an assessment of an overlay.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: The implementation specification PD-MORT-NL v4 (version 1.0, approved by the model owner on 11 June 2027) is consistent with this MDD and defines inputs, transformations, scorecards, calibration, MoC, floor and override rules for the rating engine. The handover package to Credit Risk Systems contains the implementation specification, the parameter file with final coefficients, cut-offs and grade PDs, 1,250 test cases and reference outputs produced with tag v4.0.3 of the development code. This MDD records the development code version (pd-mort-nl tag v4.0.3), the RDS version (RDS-MORT-NL-v4.0) and the parameter set (pd_mort_nl_v4_params.json, SHA-256 checksum in Annex 12) that produced the reported results. The RDS documentation, this MDD, the implementation specification and the production code are kept consistent; the reviewer compared the parameter values in this document with the parameter file and the implementation specification on 10 June 2027 without differences. After go-live the model owner confirms the consistency of production code, implementation specification and MDD after each change and at least annually in the model review.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan
sections.text: The monitoring plan of PD-MORT-NL v4 forms this chapter; it will be approved by the model owner before go-live and has been shared with Model Validation for review. It defines for each KPI the calculation, the amber and red thresholds, the quarterly frequency, the data and reference periods, the segments and grades at which it is computed, the responsible persons (monitoring analyst of Retail Credit Risk Modelling, reviewed by the model owner) and the escalation and actions per traffic light. The KPIs cover discriminatory power, calibration per grade and portfolio, score and driver stability, rating migration, production data quality, overrides, overlays and model coverage, and are computed for the whole model, per segment and per grade. The plan is updated at every model change and reviewed at least annually, and quarterly results are reported within 60 calendar days after the end of the reference quarter.

sections.heading: KPI thresholds
sections.text: Thresholds: PSI of score and drivers amber from 0.10 and red above 0.25; Gini relative decline against development amber above 10% and red above 20%, and red below 0.50 in absolute terms; Jeffreys test amber for p < 5% at portfolio level or in more than 20% of grades and red for p < 1% or in more than 30% of grades; migration by more than two grades amber above 10% and red above 20%. Model-specific override thresholds are stricter than the defaults of MRM-STD-023 §6.2: an override rate above 2% of assignments is amber and above 5% red. Model coverage is amber if more than 1% and red if more than 3% of the in-scope exposures have a missing or outdated grade, and production data quality uses the DQ rules of RDS §6.3. The thresholds for discriminatory power and calibration reflect the uncertainty of the metrics: confidence intervals are reported with each Gini value, grade-level test results are interpreted jointly with the portfolio result, and a breach of a tolerance triggers the actions of §10.3.

sections.heading: Escalation and annual review
sections.text: A red result on any KPI triggers a review by the model owner and notification of Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days; red results are reported to the Model Risk Committee. Realised default rates are compared with the grade PDs quarterly and in the annual review; where realised default rates continue to exceed the expected range, taking the economic cycle into account, the estimates are revised upward through recalibration or an overlay. A red monitoring outcome or an annual review concluding that the estimates are inadequate leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the Model Risk Committee within three months, and monitoring results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and for an additional MoC. Back-testing uses the longest available history from 2012 and the methods and data are documented in the monitoring plan and updated at least annually; changes in validation methods or data are documented.

sections.heading: Materiality, approval and challenge of expert judgement
sections.text: Each judgement is classified by its impact on the average PD and on grade assignments against the best statistical alternative: EJ-PDM4-02 and EJ-PDM4-06 are medium, the others low; the aggregate effect of all judgements is +1.9% on the average PD and a grade change for 2.6% of exposures, below the high materiality threshold of MRM-STD-023 §4.2. sections.heading: Override policy
sections.text: Overrides of the grade are permitted only within the override policy for retail mortgages: the closed list of reasons comprises OR-01 confirmed fraud, OR-02 known loss of income not yet visible in the data, OR-03 divorce or death of a co-borrower, OR-04 pending forced sale and OR-05 other information from a credit review; only downgrades of at most three grades are permitted, and upgrades are not permitted. Each override records the reason code, a written rationale, the supporting evidence, the proposer from Retail Collections and the approver from Retail Credit Risk Management, who is independent of the proposer. Override rates, direction and magnitude are monitored quarterly per reason and approving unit, and the performance of overridden obligors is compared annually with non-overridden obligors by original and final grade (see chapter 10).

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This memo describes how the Definition of Default Standard CR-STD-110 v2.0 is implemented in the systems and processes for Dutch residential mortgages (mortgage administration system, arrears management system and default register) and how the implementation is used in the reference data sets of PD-MORT-NL v4 and LGD-MORT-NL. It was prepared by Credit Risk Management at the request of Retail Credit Risk Modelling for the redevelopment of PD-MORT-NL and reflects the implementation status at 31 December 2026. Version 1.0 was reviewed by the Retail Collections process owner and approved by the Head of Credit Risk Management on 15 March 2027.

sections.heading: Days-past-due counting and materiality threshold
sections.text: Days past due are counted daily in the arrears management system at obligor level, starting on the first day on which both the absolute component of EUR 100 and the relative component of 1% are exceeded and restarting when either component is no longer exceeded; the past-due criterion is met at the onset of the 91st consecutive day. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all amounts past due of the obligor on all credit obligations to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component divides that sum by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure, excluding equity exposures. The thresholds are EUR 100 and 1% for retail exposures, as set by the ECB in Regulation (EU) 2018/1845 and applied since 31 December 2020; under CR-STD-110 v1.0 (January 2016 to December 2020) the absolute component for retail exposures was EUR 250 and the relative component 1%. Where the contractual payment schedule is modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule, and each modification is assessed by the forbearance desk for distressed restructuring. Payment holidays granted under contractual rights or by law, including the COVID-19 deferrals of 2020 granted in line with the EBA guidelines on payment moratoria, are not counted as past due, and the reason for each deferral was reviewed for indications of unlikeliness to pay.

sections.heading: Probation
sections.text: After cure, a facility remains in probation for 3 months (12 months for distressed restructurings) before returning to non-default status. The probation period starts on the day on which no past-due or UTP condition applies any longer, and the facility returns to non-default status only if, at the end of the period, the credit review of Retail Collections confirms that the improvement in the obligor's situation is factual and permanent, taking into account the payment behaviour and financial situation during probation. For exposures defaulted because of distressed restructuring, the 12-month probation starts at the latest of the restructuring measure, the default classification and the end of any grace period, and return requires regular payments totalling at least the amount previously past due or written off, no amount past due and no concern about full repayment, including under back-loaded schedules. The probation start date, probation status and end date are recorded in the default register for every default event. An obligor is returned to non-default status only when no default trigger continues to apply, and a subsequent trigger is recorded as a new default event.

sections.heading: Automatic unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The following indications lead to default automatically under CR-STD-110 §6.1: non-accrued status; a specific credit risk adjustment resulting from a significant perceived decline in credit quality, including every exposure in IFRS 9 Stage 3; the sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related economic loss above 5%; a distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%; the bankruptcy or WSNP debt restructuring of the obligor; and the forced sale of the collateral. Interest on a mortgage is no longer recognised in the income statement (non-accrued status) when the exposure is classified in Stage 3, so non-accrual coincides with the specific credit risk adjustment trigger. Allowances for losses that are not individually identified (IFRS 9 Stage 1 and Stage 2) are not treated as specific credit risk adjustments and are not a default trigger. Every exposure treated as credit-impaired is classified as defaulted, and since 2021 the IFRS 9 Stage 3 population and the prudential default population of the portfolio are identical; the exceptions of paragraph 39 of EBA/GL/2016/07 are not used.

sections.heading: Distressed restructuring and forbearance
sections.text: For each forbearance measure the forbearance desk calculates the diminished financial obligation as (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0, with the expected cash flows before and after the measure discounted at the original effective interest rate, and classifies the obligor as defaulted where it exceeds 1%. Forborne exposures below the threshold are assessed for other indications of unlikeliness to pay, in particular a large final lump sum, a back-loaded or irregular schedule, a significant grace period, repeated forbearance within 24 months or a switch from annuity to interest-only repayment. All exposures classified as forborne non-performing are classified as defaulted, which is verified monthly by comparing the forbearance register with the default register, and forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly for indications of unlikeliness to pay. In 2026 the forbearance desk assessed 1,318 forbearance measures on mortgages, of which 206 led to default because the diminished financial obligation exceeded 1% and 41 after a case-by-case assessment.

sections.heading: Sale of credit obligations
sections.text: The Bank sold non-performing residential mortgages once in the period since 2012 (a portfolio of 612 defaulted loans in November 2019); the reasons for the sale and the loss realised were analysed, and the loss was treated as credit-related. The credit-related economic loss on a sale is calculated as L = (E − P)/E, with E the outstanding amount including accrued interest and fees and P the agreed price, and obligations sold with a loss above the threshold of 5% are classified as defaulted. Where a sale at a material credit-related loss precedes the identification of default, the date of the sale is recorded as the date of default, and after a partial sale all remaining exposures to the obligor are classified as defaulted.

sections.heading: Case-by-case indications and external information
sections.text: Additional indications of unlikeliness to pay for mortgages (confirmed fraud, a significant decline in household income, unemployment or long-term illness reported by the obligor, divorce with unresolved allocation of the debt, a default registration in the BKR credit register by another lender, and repeated forbearance) trigger a case-by-case assessment by Retail Collections, completed within 30 days of detection. External information sources used are the BKR credit register (monthly), the Central Insolvency Register (daily), notifications of forced-sale procedures from the land registry (Kadaster) and public sources monitored by the fraud unit. For each indication, Annex 2 of this memo defines the identification method, the internal and external information sources, the source-system fields, the monitoring frequency and the responsible unit, and the outcome of each case-by-case assessment is recorded in the default register with its rationale. Case-by-case assessments follow written labelling guidelines with decision criteria per indication, and a quarterly quality review of 50 closed cases by Credit Risk Management checks for systematic differences between assessors; the review of Q4 2026 found no significant differences.

sections.heading: Joint obligations and contagion
sections.text: Joint credit obligations of partners are treated as a separate obligor; when a joint obligation defaults, the individual exposures of each partner (for example a personal loan or credit card) are also classified as defaulted unless the Bank demonstrates that this is not justified, in which case the rationale is recorded. Default of one obligor does not automatically affect connected obligors in the retail mortgage portfolio; contagion within a group of connected clients, such as a self-employed obligor and his or her company, is assessed case by case by Retail Collections using the criteria of section 8 of EBA/GL/2016/07. Because the definition is applied at obligor level for all retail exposures, the facility-level provisions of paragraphs 92–93 of EBA/GL/2016/07 are not used.
