sections.heading: Technical past due and disputed obligations
sections.text: A past-due situation is treated as technical past due only where it results from an error of the Bank's data or payment systems, the failure of a payment instruction executed by the obligor, or the time lag in allocating a payment received; a wrong credit decision or an error in the loan agreement never qualifies as technical past due. Each technical past due case is documented, corrected within 30 days and reviewed quarterly by Credit Risk Management, and corrected cases are removed from the default events delivered to the reference data sets. Days-past-due counting is suspended for a disputed amount only where the dispute has been brought before a court or before the Dutch financial services complaints institute (Kifid) under a binding procedure. Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date is recognised as a past-due credit obligation. In 2026, 37 technical past due cases were recorded for mortgages, all caused by payment allocation delays after an interest-rate reset.

sections.heading: Identification process, timeliness and consistency across systems
sections.text: Days-past-due counting and the automatic triggers are processed daily by the arrears management system, and the manual processes (case-by-case assessments, the forborne exposure list, the watch list and specific credit risk adjustments) are updated at least weekly, which ensures timely identification of default. Once the past-due criterion is met, the obligor is classified as defaulted automatically, without further expert judgement, and all its exposures are flagged as defaulted. The default status is maintained at obligor level in the default register and propagated daily to the mortgage administration system, the consumer credit systems and the risk data warehouse, so that the default of an obligor is identified consistently across all IT systems of the Bank's Dutch retail entity. The date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met and is recorded for every default event, also where the default is identified after that date. There are no legal impediments to the exchange of client data within the group for the retail mortgage portfolio.

sections.heading: Consistent application and use
sections.text: The same definition of default applies to all retail exposures of the Bank and its subsidiaries and is used for own funds requirements, IFRS 9 Stage 3, non-performing exposure reporting, arrears management and internal risk reporting to the Management Board. The PD and LGD models of the retail mortgage rating system use the same default events from the default register. IRB and IFRS 9 default flags are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems by Credit Risk Reporting. Differences between the default register and the accounting classification found in these reconciliations are resolved within the quarter.

sections.heading: Monitoring of the return to non-default status
sections.text: Credit Risk Management analyses annually, per default trigger, cure rates, the share of obligors returning to non-default status and re-default rates within 12 and 24 months after return; the analysis for 2026 shows a 12-month re-default rate of 6.8% after the 3-month probation and 4.1% after the 12-month probation for restructured exposures. Both rates are below the internal trigger of 10% at which a longer probation period is proposed, so the probation periods were not changed; the results are reported to the Credit Risk Committee.

documents.title: Model change memorandum PD-MORT-NL v3 to v4 (CHG-2026-0417)

sections.heading: Change identification and summary
sections.text: The redevelopment of PD-MORT-NL from v3 to v4 has been recorded in the change log of the model inventory as change CHG-2026-0417 since 22 September 2026, before any implementation in production. The change affects the rating system for Dutch owner-occupied residential mortgages, which at 31 December 2026 covers 376,900 facilities of 164,300 obligors with an EAD of EUR 37.4 billion and RWEA of EUR 4,436 million, and implementation is planned at the first month-end at least one month after the ECB permission, expected in the third quarter of 2028. This memorandum follows MRM-STD-050 §4.2 and is approved by the model owner; the classification was confirmed by Model Risk Management on 8 June 2027.

evidence.quote: The redevelopment of PD-MORT-NL from v3 to v4 has been recorded in the change log of the model inventory as change CHG-2026-0417 since 22 September 2026, before any implementation in production.

sections.heading: Description and rationale of the change
sections.text: The change consists of an extended observation period (2012–2024 instead of 2012–2019), a segmented model structure with two scorecards, new and removed risk drivers, recalibration to the extended long-run average and a re-quantified margin of conservatism under CRM-STD-101 v2.0. Its objectives are to address findings V3-F01 (calibration of obligors in arrears) and V3-F02 (representativeness for self-employed obligors) of the 2025 validation of v3, to use five additional years of data collected under the current definition of default, to reflect the growing share of loans originated under the stricter lending standards since 2013, and to replace the post-model adjustment for interest-only loans applied to v3 since 2025. Pending the permission for v4, the deficiencies of v3 identified by validation are mitigated by the post-model adjustment OV-2025-02 and by an additional MoC for the arrears grades, and the redevelopment is the plan to restore full compliance, with its timeline included in the IRB remediation plan shared with the Joint Supervisory Team in 2026. The master scale, the definition of default, the override policy and the rating philosophy are unchanged.

sections.heading: Regulatory classification
sections.text: Under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 the change is material (class A) and requires prior permission of the ECB under CRR Art. 143(3), because the new rating criteria change the rank ordering significantly (Annex I, Part II, Section 1, point 2(d)) and because the MoC methodology changes (point 2(f)). The Bank's change policy defines the measures and significance levels for point 2(d): a change of rating criteria is significant where the Spearman rank correlation between old and new scores is below 0.90 or more than 10% of exposures move by more than one grade; the observed values are 0.86 and 9.8%. The other qualitative criteria are not met: the rating philosophy (point 2(c)) and the definition of default (point 3) are unchanged. The extension of the time series beyond the annual inclusion of the latest observations would on its own require ex ante notification (Annex I, Part II, Section 2, point 5(c)); it is covered by the application for the material change.

sections.heading: Quantitative impact
sections.text: The impact was calculated at the most recent reference date, 31 December 2026, by rating the same exposures with v3 and v4 while holding EAD, LGD and all other parameters constant: the RWEA of the range of application decreases from EUR 4,436 million to EUR 4,254 million (−4.1%), and the Bank's total credit and dilution risk RWEA of EUR 38.9 billion at the highest level of consolidation decreases by 0.47%. Both decreases are below the quantitative thresholds for material changes (1.5% overall and 15% for the range of application) and below the 5% threshold for ex ante notification. The impact was calculated on the full portfolio, so no sample-based inference was needed. The average PD after MoC decreases from 0.58% to 0.53%; 34.6% of exposures change grade (18.1% to a better and 16.5% to a worse grade) and 9.8% move by more than one grade.

sections.heading: Portfolio development and model coverage
sections.text: At the start of the observation period (31 December 2025) the portfolio comprised 373,200 facilities of 162,900 obligors, EAD EUR 36.1 billion and RWEA EUR 4,301 million in 12 non-defaulted grades; at the end (31 December 2026) 376,900 facilities of 164,300 obligors, EAD EUR 37.4 billion and RWEA EUR 4,436 million; 612 obligors defaulted during 2026. Model coverage was 99.6% of the in-scope exposures; the remaining 0.4% were loans in their first month after origination without a behavioural grade, no rating was older than one month, no ratings were transferred and no obligors were excluded because of rating process deficiencies. Ratings are refreshed monthly for every obligor, so all retail assignments are updated at least annually. The share of new loans with an interest-only part fell further to 9% of new production, and no new mortgage products were introduced in 2026, so the appropriateness of the internal approach is not affected by new products.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: The Gini coefficient on the 2026 observation period is 0.738 against 0.768 at the initial validation (relative decline 3.9%, below the 10% amber threshold and above the absolute red threshold of 0.50 for retail rating models). The ECB test on the change in AUC (AUC 0.884 at initial validation against 0.869, standard error 0.0069, S = 2.17, p-value 0.015) indicates a significant decrease and is rated amber, as in 2025. The analysis was performed on the whole application portfolio without development exclusions, and the decrease is concentrated among obligors in arrears, where the Gini fell from 0.61 to 0.55.

sections.heading: Calibration and back-testing
sections.text: Realised default rates were compared with the PD per grade and for the portfolio with the one-sided Jeffreys test of MV-HB-003: at portfolio level the average PD of 0.58% exceeds the default rate of 0.37% (p = 1.00), while grades R10 and R11 show p-values of 0.021 and 0.034, i.e. 2 of 12 grades (17%) below 5%, which is green under the thresholds of MRM-STD-040 §5.4. The deviations in R10 and R11 are analysed: they concern obligors in arrears whose default rates exceed the grade PD, the pattern behind finding V3-F01, and they are covered by the additional MoC for the arrears grades until v4 is implemented. Back-testing covers the full history since 2012 per grade and per year, and the methods and data are unchanged from previous reviews and are documented in the monitoring plan. Including the default data of 2020–2025 would lower the long-run average default rate of v3 from 0.54% to 0.44%, a material change that requires recalibration, which is performed in v4.

sections.heading: Stability and migration
sections.text: The PSI of the grade distribution against the v3 development sample is 0.09 (green); among the risk drivers the interest-only flag (0.14) and original LTV (0.11) are amber because of the shift towards amortising loans with lower LTV, which is explained by the stricter lending standards since 2013. The 12-month migration matrix shows 80.4% of obligors in the same grade and 2.4% migrating by more than two grades; the upper and lower matrix weighted bandwidths are 0.21 and 0.18. Pairwise z-tests on the monotonicity of off-diagonal transition frequencies show no significant violation for any grade. The number-weighted Herfindahl index is 0.21 against 0.19 at initial validation (p-value of the coefficient-of-variation test 0.12), and the exposure-weighted index is 0.23.

sections.heading: Overrides
sections.text: In 2026, 312 obligors (0.19% of the validation sample, all downgrades) were overridden, far below the model-specific amber threshold of 2% and the 5% review threshold of CR-POL-001 §7.4 for retail rating systems. By reason, 48% were OR-02 (known income loss), 27% OR-03 (divorce or death of a co-borrower), 11% OR-04 (pending forced sale), 9% OR-01 (fraud) and 5% OR-05; the average override was 1.6 grades, and 92% were approved by the retail credit risk desk and 8% by the Head of Retail Credit Risk Management. The default rate of overridden obligors was 9.8% against 0.37% for non-overridden obligors, and by original grade overridden obligors defaulted more often than non-overridden obligors of the same grade, while by final grade their default rates were in line with the grade PD; the overrides therefore improved risk differentiation and do not indicate a systematic model deficiency.

sections.heading: Overlays and post-model adjustments
sections.text: Post-model adjustment OV-2025-02 (+7% relative on the PD of facilities with an interest-only share above 50% and a remaining term below ten years) addresses limitation L3-06 of v3 on the refinancing risk of interest-only loans; it was quantified with the default rates of interest-only loans in the last five years of their term, approved by the Model Risk Committee on 26 June 2025 and adds EUR 134 million RWEA. The overlay was reassessed in every quarter of 2026 and is reported quarterly to the Model Risk Committee; its planned removal date is the implementation of v4, which captures the interest-only share as a risk driver. Because the overlay will have been in place for more than 24 months by June 2027, the model change assessment required by MRM-STD-023 §3.5 is covered by change CHG-2026-0417.

sections.heading: Annual review of estimates and representativeness
sections.text: The annual review of estimates covers back-testing, representativeness, the need for recalibration and the adequacy of the MoC, using predefined metrics and thresholds and predefined actions for adverse results as set out in the monitoring plan. Representativeness of the v3 development data for the 2026 portfolio was analysed for the range of application, the definition of default and the risk drivers: the range of application is unchanged, the default definition of v3 data (2012–2019) differs from the current definition for 2012–2015, and the amber PSI values of §6 reflect the portfolio shift since 2013. Data adjustments and exclusions in the review follow the same rules as in the RDS of v3. The review concludes that v3 remains fit for purpose until v4 is implemented, subject to the overlay OV-2025-02 and the additional MoC for the arrears grades, and that the estimates must be recalibrated; the conclusion was signed off by the model owner on 26 March 2027 and submitted to Model Risk Management and Model Validation.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and approval
sections.text: This implementation specification defines the production implementation of PD-MORT-NL v4 in the Bank's credit risk rating engine and is consistent with the approved MDD version 4.0; it was prepared before implementation started and was approved by the model owner on 11 June 2027. It forms part of the handover package to Credit Risk Systems together with the parameter file, 1,250 test cases and the reference outputs produced with tag v4.0.3 of the development code. Implementation by Credit Risk Systems starts after gate G1; go-live is planned after the ECB permission.

sections.heading: Production architecture and version control
sections.text: The model runs monthly in the credit risk rating engine, which also computes exposure values and risk weights for the own funds calculation; the engine implements the IRB risk-weight formula for retail exposures secured by residential property and is regression-tested at every release. Development code (repository pd-mort-nl) and production code (repository cre-models, module pd_mort_nl_v4) are held in the Bank's approved version control system, and every version used for reported or production outputs is tagged and retrievable. Parameter tables (bins, weights of evidence, coefficients, score cut-offs, grade PDs, MoC add-ons and the floor) are loaded from a version-controlled parameter file with restricted write access and are changed only through change management. Model developers have read-only access to the production environment, and deployments are performed by the release team of Credit Risk Systems. Changes to production code follow the Bank's change management with four-eyes code review by a developer other than the author and documented approval before deployment; emergency changes deployed before completion of all tests require approval by the model owner and Model Risk Management, and the outstanding tests are completed within 30 calendar days.

sections.heading: Transformations, missing values and outliers
sections.text: Annex 2 specifies every transformation (binning, weights of evidence, calculation of the indexed LTV), the missing-value treatment per variable (median imputation of debt-to-income at origination by origination year, a separate bin for months since last cure), the capping of indexed LTV at 250%, and every formula, coefficient, lookup table, master scale mapping, MoC add-on, floor and override rule, with double-precision arithmetic and rounding of the final PD to six decimals. Outliers are identified with the same criteria in development and production (indexed LTV above 250%, debt-to-income at origination above 60%), and the capping is applied identically in both.

sections.heading: Calibration, MoC and floor in production
sections.text: Production applies the steps in the documented order: score per segment, calibrated best-estimate PD and grade assignment, override, MoC add-on per grade and the PD floor of 0.05% at exposure level. The share of exposures and EAD to which the floor is binding is reported monthly by the engine. For the interface to the IFRS 9 engine, the rating engine delivers the grade and the best-estimate PD without MoC and floor.

sections.heading: Overrides in production
sections.text: The override screen in the collections workflow allows only reason codes OR-01 to OR-05 and downgrades of at most three grades, requires a written rationale and a supporting document, and routes each override to an approver in Retail Credit Risk Management other than the proposer. The engine records for each override the original and final grade, the reason code, the proposer, the approver and the dates, which form the basis of the override monitoring.

sections.heading: Reconciliation
sections.text: Production outputs will be reconciled at record level with the outputs of the development code on identical input data, covering the full December 2024 snapshot of the RDS and the production snapshot of the month before go-live. The tolerances are an absolute difference of at most 10^-6 or a relative difference of at most 0.01% for scores and PDs, and an identical segment and grade for all records; differences outside tolerance are investigated and explained, and any unexplained difference blocks go-live. Model outputs will be reconciled with the downstream systems (own funds calculation, IFRS 9 engine, collections workflow and pricing tool) at go-live and at least annually thereafter.

sections.text: A parallel run of v3 and v4 will cover three consecutive monthly reference dates, including a full quarter-end own funds cycle, before v4 is used for decisions or regulatory reporting. The parallel run report will analyse grade migration between v3 and v4, the impact on RWEA and expected loss, the effect on collections prioritisation and operational issues.

sections.heading: Production controls
sections.text: Each production run is logged with reference date, input data version, code version and parameter file checksum, and the engine refuses to run with a code or parameter version that is not registered as approved. Manual reruns, manual output adjustments and fallback procedures (use of the previous month's grade if input data fail validation) are documented in the run book, require authorisation by the model owner and are logged. Outputs used for regulatory reporting are retained for ten years together with the input data and the code version used to produce them. Before each run, production input data are checked for completeness and validity with the DQ rules applied to the RDS (RDS documentation §6.3).

deficiencies.rationale: MDD §7.2 and §6.2 link the approximated default flag 2012–2015 to MoC category A (+6% relative), but the +6% rests on a single overlap-year comparison (2016) of the days-past-due criterion; an independent sensitivity analysis that also reflects the case-by-case UTP defaults not captured before 2016 indicates that about +11% is needed.

mitigation.text: Re-quantify MoC A1 with a sensitivity analysis covering all default triggers and alternative reconstructions of the 2012–2015 default flag; if the total MoC then exceeds 20% of the best estimate, present the need for redevelopment to the MRC (CRM-STD-101 §7.2).

deficiencies.rationale: The DoD implementation memo §3 describes the probation periods (3 months, 12 months after distressed restructuring), but not the treatment of obligors that default again within 12 months of returning to non-default status, which CR-STD-110 §8.1 requires to be merged into a single default for risk parameter estimation.

mitigation.text: Document the treatment of multiple defaults within 12 months after cure in the memo and in RDS chapter 3, and report the number of merged default events in the RDS (CR-STD-110 §8.2).

deficiencies.rationale: RDS §2.2 states that the window includes the 2012–2013 downturn, but does not demonstrate that the share of bad years in the window is representative of the long run.

mitigation.text: Add a comparison of the yearly default rates with a longer macroeconomic series (house prices and unemployment 2000–2024) and classify the years of the window as good or bad.

deficiencies.rationale: RDS §5.1 and Annex B compare risk-driver distributions (PSI 0.04–0.06 and the full LTV distribution), but default-rate levels of the RDS are not compared with those of the current portfolio per segment.

mitigation.text: Add a comparison of default rates per segment and grade between the RDS and the portfolio of 2022–2024, with a two-sample test of proportions.

deficiencies.rationale: RDS §6.1 and §6.4 assess completeness, accuracy, consistency, validity and uniqueness, but not the timeliness dimension of MRM-STD-022 (refresh lag of the source systems and currency of collateral values).

mitigation.text: Add a timeliness assessment per source system (lag between reference date and availability) and for periodically refreshed items such as collateral valuations.

deficiencies.rationale: MoC A2 and A3 are supported by re-estimation under alternative treatments, but MoC A1 (+6%) is derived from the default count ratio in the 2016 overlap year only; no re-estimation of the long-run average under plausible alternative reconstructions of the 2012–2015 default flag is documented.

mitigation.text: Document a sensitivity analysis for MoC A1 that re-estimates the long-run average under alternative approximation rules and states the range and the value selected (CRM-STD-101 §5.3).
